preamble: An Act to define and amend certain parts of the law relating to contracts. Preamble: WHEREAS it is expedient to define and amend certain parts of the law relating to contracts; It is hereby enacted as follows:—

glossary.agreements: A mutual understanding between two or more parties about their rights and duties. Not every agreement is legally enforceable — only those meeting the tests in Section 10 become contracts.
glossary.free consent: Agreement given without being forced, tricked, pressured, or mistaken. Section 14 lists five things that can spoil consent: coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, and mistake.
glossary.competent to contract: Legally capable of entering into a binding agreement. Section 11 sets three requirements: the person must have reached the age of majority, be of sound mind, and not be barred by any other law.
glossary.lawful consideration: Something of value — money, a promise, an object, or an act — exchanged between the parties, as long as it isn't illegal, immoral, or against public policy.
glossary.lawful object: The purpose of the agreement must not be forbidden by law, fraudulent, injurious to another person or their property, immoral, or against public policy.
glossary.void: Having no legal effect at all — a void agreement cannot be enforced by either party in any court, as if it never created any rights or obligations.
glossary.age of majority: The age at which a person is legally treated as an adult. Under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, this is ordinarily 18 years (or 21 years if a guardian has been appointed for the person or their property).
glossary.sound mind: The mental capacity, at the moment of contracting, to understand the agreement's terms and to form a rational judgment about how it will affect one's own interests. This is tested at the time of the transaction, not as a permanent label on the person.
glossary.unsound mind: A mental state in which a person is incapable of understanding the nature and consequences of their acts.
glossary.rational judgment: The ability to weigh how an agreement will help or harm one's own interests, not merely the ability to understand its words.
glossary.saving clause: A provision that protects certain existing rights, laws, or practices from being affected by a new statute, so they continue to operate unless expressly overridden.
glossary.proposal: An offer — one person signalling to another their willingness to do or not do something, in order to get that other person's agreement to it. Called a 'promise' once accepted.
glossary.acceptance: The offeree's clear agreement to a proposal, given in the manner asked for (or a reasonable manner). It must exactly match the proposal — any change turns it into a counter-offer instead.
glossary.promisor: The person who makes a proposal that is accepted, and who therefore owes the resulting promise.
glossary.promisee: The person who accepts a proposal, and who is therefore owed the resulting promise.
glossary.consideration: What each side gives or promises in exchange for the other's promise — money, an act, forbearance, or another promise — done at the desire of the promisor.
glossary.reciprocal promises: Promises that form the consideration, or part of the consideration, for each other — each side's promise is the price of the other's.
glossary.contract: An agreement that the law will enforce.
glossary.voidable contract: A contract that remains fully valid and binding unless and until the wronged party chooses to cancel it — unlike a void agreement, which was never enforceable at all.
glossary.communication of proposal: The point at which an offer, acceptance, or its revocation legally takes effect — governed by precise rules in Sections 3 to 5, since a proposal, an acceptance, and a revocation can each become 'complete' at a different moment for each party.
glossary.communication when complete: The specific moment at which a proposal, acceptance, or revocation becomes legally effective — which can differ depending on whether you are the sender or the receiver.
glossary.revocation: Withdrawing a proposal or an acceptance before it becomes legally binding. Once communication is 'complete' against a party, that party can no longer revoke.
glossary.express promise: A promise stated explicitly, in words, whether oral or written.
glossary.implied promise: A promise inferred from conduct or circumstances rather than stated explicitly.
glossary.consent: Agreement between two or more people on the very same thing, understood in the very same sense by both.
glossary.consensus ad idem: Latin for 'agreement as to the same thing' — the legal requirement that both parties understand the terms of their agreement identically.
glossary.coercion: Forcing someone into an agreement by committing or threatening an act that the criminal law forbids, or by unlawfully detaining or threatening to detain their property.
glossary.undue influence: Using a position of dominance over someone's will — such as authority, a fiduciary relationship, or their impaired mental state — to obtain an unfair advantage from them in a contract.
glossary.fiduciary relation: A relationship of trust and confidence (such as trustee-beneficiary, guardian-ward, or doctor-patient) in which one party is expected to act in the other's best interests.
glossary.unconscionable: So one-sided or unfair that it shocks the conscience of the court — a key trigger under Section 16(3) for shifting the burden of proof onto the dominant party.
glossary.fraud: A dishonest act intended to deceive another and induce them to act to their detriment.
glossary.active concealment: Deliberately hiding a fact one knows or believes to be true, in order to deceive the other party — distinct from mere silence.
glossary.mere silence: Simply not volunteering information. Under Section 17's Explanation, silence alone is not fraud unless there was a duty to speak, or the silence was itself equivalent to a false statement.
glossary.misrepresentation: A false statement of fact made by one party that induces another to enter into a contract.
glossary.coercion, fraud or misrepresentation: The three consent-vitiating grounds under Section 19 that make a contract voidable at the option of the wronged party.
glossary.mistake of fact: A false belief about a factual matter essential to the agreement — for example, believing goods still exist when they have already been destroyed.
glossary.common mistake: A mistake of fact shared by both parties to the agreement — under Section 20, this voids the agreement entirely if the fact was essential to it.
glossary.unilateral mistake: A mistake of fact held by only one of the two parties — under Section 22, this alone does not make the contract voidable.
glossary.mistake of law: A false belief about what the law provides. A mistake about Indian law gives no relief; a mistake about foreign law is treated the same as a mistake of fact.
glossary.public policy: The body of interests that courts protect against private bargains — such as preventing corruption, protecting the administration of justice, and safeguarding personal freedoms like marriage and trade.
glossary.natural love and affection: The emotional bond between close relatives, which Section 25 recognises as a valid basis for an enforceable gift-like promise, but only if the promise is also in writing and registered.
glossary.restraint of marriage: A contract term that limits or penalises a person's freedom to marry — void under Section 26 for any person who is not a minor.
glossary.restraint of trade: A contract term restricting a person's ability to carry on a lawful profession, trade, or business — void under Section 27 except for the narrow good-will exception.
glossary.good-will: The reputation and customer loyalty attached to a business, which can be sold along with a valid, reasonably limited promise by the seller not to compete with the buyer.
glossary.restraint of legal proceedings: A contract term that blocks a party from going to court, or artificially shortens their time to sue, or strips their rights merely because time has passed — void under Section 28, apart from the arbitration exceptions.
glossary.arbitration: A private dispute-resolution process, agreed to by contract, in which a neutral arbitrator decides the dispute instead of a court — expressly protected from Section 28's general bar on restraining legal proceedings.
glossary.uncertainty: A degree of vagueness in an agreement's terms that cannot be resolved even by looking at context, trade custom, or an agreed mechanism — Section 29 voids only agreements this vague.
glossary.wager: A bet — an agreement where each side's gain or loss depends purely on the outcome of an uncertain event, with no other stake in that outcome. Wagering agreements are void and unenforceable in court under Section 30.
glossary.contingent contract: A contract to do or not do something if an uncertain future event, collateral to the contract, does or does not happen — e.g. an insurance policy that pays only if a specified event occurs.
glossary.performance: Actually carrying out what a party promised under a contract — paying money owed, delivering goods, rendering a service, etc.
glossary.representatives: Persons who legally stand in the place of a deceased or incapacitated person, such as heirs, executors, or guardians.
glossary.tender of performance: A valid, properly-made offer to perform a contractual obligation (unconditional, at the proper time/place, with a reasonable opportunity to verify) which, if refused by the other side, discharges the person who made the offer from liability for non-performance.
glossary.joint promisees: Two or more persons to whom a single promise is made together, who must generally act jointly to enforce it.
glossary.repudiation: A clear refusal by a party, through words or conduct, to perform his contractual obligations at all.
glossary.acquiescence: Accepting or going along with a state of affairs (such as continued performance after a breach) by words or conduct, which can result in losing the right to treat the contract as terminated.
glossary.joint promise: A promise made by two or more persons together, making them jointly answerable to the promisee unless the contract says otherwise.
glossary.contribution: The right of a person who has paid more than his share of a joint obligation to recover the excess proportionately from his co-obligors.
glossary.surety: A person who guarantees the performance of another's (the principal debtor's) obligation, and who becomes liable if the principal fails to perform.
glossary.release: A promisee's act of giving up or discharging his claim against one of several parties who owe him an obligation.
glossary.reasonable time: A flexible, fact-specific standard used when a contract fixes no deadline for performance — determined by the nature of the obligation, trade custom, and the parties' circumstances, not a fixed legal period.
glossary.agreement: Every promise, or set of reciprocal promises, forming the consideration for each other — the broader category of which a legally enforceable "contract" is a subset (Section 2(e), (h)).
glossary.mistake: An erroneous belief held by one or both parties about a fact or law relevant to the agreement at the time of contracting — see "mistake of fact" and "mistake of law" for how the Act treats each differently.
glossary.time is of the essence: A contractual term meaning that a stated deadline for performance is strictly binding — missing it entitles the innocent party to treat the contract as voidable, rather than merely claim compensation for delay.
glossary.impossibility: A supervening event, occurring after a contract is validly made, that renders the promised performance impossible or unlawful — this doctrine (sometimes called frustration) can render the contract void from the point impossibility arises.
glossary.novation: Substituting an entirely new contract for an existing one — often by replacing one of the original parties with a new party — by mutual agreement of everyone involved, discharging the original contract.
glossary.rescission: Cancelling or setting aside a contract, either because it is voidable at one party's option, or by the parties' mutual agreement, so that it no longer needs to be performed.
glossary.restitution: Restoring a benefit received under a contract or agreement (or paying its value) to the person from whom it was received, typically because the underlying agreement is void, voidable and rescinded, or otherwise unenforceable.
glossary.appropriation of payment: The process of deciding which of several debts owed by the same debtor to the same creditor a particular payment is credited against.
glossary.quasi-contract: An obligation the law imposes on a person even though no real contract exists between the parties, in order to prevent one person from being unjustly enriched at another's expense.
glossary.necessaries: Goods or services suited to a person's actual condition and station in life that are reasonably essential for his (or his dependants') support — a special category relevant when supplied to a person legally incapable of contracting.
glossary.bailee: The person to whom goods are delivered under a bailment.
glossary.penalty: A sum of money, or other stipulation, named in a contract as payable on breach that is not a genuine pre-estimate of loss but is intended to punish or deter the defaulting party — Indian law caps recovery under such a clause at reasonable compensation, regardless of the sum named.
glossary.liquidated damages: A sum fixed in advance by the contracting parties as the compensation payable on a specified breach — under Section 74, Indian courts treat this the same as a penalty clause and award only reasonable compensation up to that sum.
glossary.remote and indirect loss: Loss or damage flowing from a breach of contract that is too distant, speculative, or indirect a consequence of the breach to be recoverable as compensation under Section 73.
glossary.compensation: A payment made to make good a loss or injury suffered by another.
glossary.contract of indemnity: A contract by which one party (the indemnifier) promises to save the other (the indemnity-holder) from loss caused by the indemnifier's own conduct or by the conduct of a third person.
glossary.indemnity-holder: The promisee under a contract of indemnity — the person protected against loss, entitled to recover damages, costs, and reasonable settlement sums from the indemnifier once the covered loss materialises.
glossary.contract of guarantee: A contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person (the principal debtor) in case of his default; may be oral or written.
glossary.principal debtor: The person whose debt or duty is guaranteed by a surety, and in respect of whose default the guarantee is given.
glossary.creditor: The person to whom a guarantee is given — the party entitled to enforce the guaranteed debt or duty against either the principal debtor or the surety.
glossary.continuing guarantee: A guarantee that extends to an open-ended series of transactions (such as ongoing credit supply), rather than being limited to a single specific transaction.
glossary.co-sureties: Two or more sureties who have each guaranteed the same debt or duty, whether under the same contract or separate ones, and whether or not they know of each other — they owe each other a duty of equal contribution by default.
glossary.subrogation: The legal mechanism by which a surety who pays off a guaranteed debt automatically steps into the creditor's shoes, acquiring all the rights (and the benefit of any security) the creditor had against the principal debtor.
glossary.concealment: A creditor's silence as to material circumstances bearing on the risk a surety is asked to guarantee — unlike ordinary contracting parties, a creditor's concealment of such circumstances can itself invalidate the resulting guarantee.
glossary.bailment: The delivery of goods by one person (the bailor) to another (the bailee) for a purpose, on the understanding that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of once that purpose is accomplished. Ownership does not transfer; only possession does.
glossary.bailor: The person who delivers goods to another under a bailment.
glossary.gratuitous bailment: A bailment made without any charge or reward to either party — a free loan or free keeping of goods.
glossary.lien: A right to retain possession of another's goods until a debt or charge relating to those goods is paid.
glossary.particular lien: A right to retain specific goods only until charges relating to work done on those particular goods are paid (Section 170).
glossary.general lien: A broader right, available only to specified professionals (bankers, factors, wharfingers, High Court attorneys, policy-brokers), to retain goods as security for the entire outstanding balance owed, not just charges tied to those specific goods (Section 171).
glossary.pledge: The bailment of goods as security for the payment of a debt or the performance of a promise.
glossary.pawnor: The person who bails (pledges) goods as security for a debt or promise.
glossary.pawnee: The person who receives goods pledged as security for a debt or promise.
glossary.mercantile agent: An agent who, in the customary course of his business, has authority either to sell goods, or to consign goods for sale, or to buy goods, or to raise money on the security of goods, on behalf of another.
glossary.finder of goods: A person who finds lost goods belonging to another; treated by the Act broadly like a bailee, with a right to retain the goods for compensation of trouble/expense and, where a specific reward is offered, a right to sue for it.
glossary.delivery of goods: The act of handing over possession of goods from one person to another, whether physically or by any act that puts the goods within the other's control.
glossary.delivery: The act of putting goods into the possession of another person, or of someone authorized to hold them on that person's behalf.
glossary.possession: The state of having control over goods, whether or not one owns them.
glossary.bailment for hire: A bailment made in exchange for payment (reward) to the bailor, as opposed to a gratuitous bailment.
glossary.disclosure: The duty to reveal known facts — here, faults in bailed goods — to the other party.
glossary.material fault: A defect in goods that meaningfully interferes with their intended use or exposes the user to extraordinary risk, as opposed to a trivial or harmless flaw.
glossary.ordinary prudence: The level of care and caution that a reasonable, sensible person would exercise in looking after his own property.
glossary.standard of care: The degree of caution and diligence a person is legally required to exercise in a given situation.
glossary.special contract: A specific agreement between parties that varies or displaces a default statutory rule.
glossary.avoidable: Capable of being treated as void, at the option of one party, rather than being automatically void or continuing to bind both parties.
glossary.inconsistent act: An act by the bailee regarding the bailed goods that departs from the conditions on which the bailment was made.
glossary.unauthorized use: Use of bailed goods in a manner not permitted by the conditions of the bailment.
glossary.mixture: The combining or blending of the bailor's goods with the bailee's own goods, whether with or without the bailor's consent.
glossary.proportionate interest: A share in mixed or combined property calculated according to each party's original contribution.
glossary.separation: The physical dividing of mixed goods back into the distinct portions originally belonging to each party.
glossary.necessary expenses: Reasonable, ordinary costs genuinely required for the purpose of a bailment or pledge, such as the upkeep of the goods.
glossary.borrower: A person who receives a thing from another (the lender) for temporary use, under a loan.
glossary.indemnify: To compensate a person for loss or damage they have suffered or may suffer.
glossary.return of goods: The bailee's act of giving the bailed goods back to the bailor, or dealing with them as the bailor directs, once the bailment ends.
glossary.default: A failure to perform an obligation by the time or in the manner required, such as failing to pay a debt or return goods on time.
glossary.responsibility: Legal liability for loss, damage, or harm arising from one's own act, omission, or default.
glossary.termination: The ending of a legal relationship or obligation, such as a bailment.
glossary.increase or profit: Any natural growth, produce, or benefit generated by bailed property while it is in the bailee's custody, such as the offspring of a bailed animal.
glossary.joint owners: Two or more persons who together own the same property, each holding an undivided interest in it.
glossary.good faith: Honest intention and genuine belief in the propriety of one's actions, without knowledge of any defect or fraud.
glossary.title: A person's legal right of ownership over property.
glossary.third person: Someone who is not a party to the bailment or contract in question, such as a stranger asserting a competing claim to bailed goods.
glossary.specific reward: A particular, identified reward publicly offered by an owner for the return of lost property.
glossary.lawful charges: Legitimate expenses or costs that a person, such as a finder of goods, is entitled to recover or be reimbursed for.
glossary.labour or skill: Work or expertise applied by a bailee to bailed goods, such as cutting, polishing, repairing, or crafting them.
glossary.attorney: A legal practitioner authorized to act on behalf of clients before a court, such as a High Court.
glossary.banker: A person or institution carrying on the business of banking, including receiving deposits and lending money.
glossary.factor: A mercantile agent entrusted with the possession of goods for the purpose of selling them on behalf of the owner.
glossary.policy-broker: An agent who arranges insurance policies on behalf of clients with insurers.
glossary.wharfinger: A person who owns or manages a wharf and takes charge of goods landed there.
glossary.retainer: The act of holding onto goods as security until a debt, charge, or expense connected with them is paid.
glossary.subsequent advances: Further loans or sums of money advanced by a lender to a borrower after the original debt or pledge, in addition to the original amount.
glossary.extraordinary expenses: Unusual, above-normal costs incurred to preserve pledged goods, beyond the ordinary necessary expenses of keeping them.
glossary.sale of pledge: The pawnee's remedy, after giving reasonable notice, of selling pledged goods to recover a debt on the pawnor's default.
glossary.redeem: To reclaim pledged goods by paying the debt or fulfilling the promise for which they were pledged.
glossary.document of title: A document (such as a bill of lading or warehouse receipt) that in the ordinary course of business is treated as proof of possession or control of goods, and whose transfer operates to transfer that possession or control.
glossary.limited interest: A partial or restricted ownership interest in property, short of full/absolute ownership — for example, a co-owner's share or a lessee's interest.
glossary.wrong-doer: A person who, without legal right, interferes with, damages, or wrongfully deprives another of possession of property.
glossary.apportionment: The fair division of relief, compensation, or proceeds among two or more persons according to their respective interests.
glossary.agent: A person employed to do an act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third persons.
glossary.principal: The person for whom an act is done, or who is represented, by an agent.
glossary.express authority: Authority given to an agent by words, spoken or written.
glossary.implied authority: Authority inferred from the circumstances of the case, including conduct, the ordinary course of dealing, or things spoken or written.
glossary.course of dealing: A pattern of prior conduct between two parties that can be taken into account in inferring the existence or scope of an agent's authority.
glossary.incidental powers: Powers an agent is taken to have by necessary implication, even without express mention, because they are necessary to carry out an authorized act or business.
glossary.emergency: A sudden, unforeseen situation requiring urgent action, in which an agent may act beyond his ordinary instructions to protect the principal from loss.
glossary.delegate: To hand over performance of a task or duty to another person.
glossary.sub-agent: A person employed by, and acting under the control of, an original agent in the business of the agency.
glossary.wilful wrong: A deliberate, knowing act of wrongdoing, as opposed to mere carelessness or negligence.
glossary.unauthorized appointment: The appointment of a sub-agent or substitute by an agent who lacked the authority to make such an appointment.
glossary.substituted agent: A person named by an agent, under express or implied authority to do so, who becomes a direct agent of the principal (not a sub-agent under the original agent's control) for the part of the business entrusted to him.
glossary.discretion: The judgment and care a person exercises in making a decision, particularly in selecting another person to act on one's behalf.
glossary.ratification: The act of adopting and confirming, after the fact, an act done on one's behalf without prior authority — giving it the same legal effect as if it had been authorized from the start.
glossary.unauthorized act: An act done by one person on behalf of another without that other person's knowledge or authority.
glossary.implied ratification: Ratification inferred from a person's conduct after an unauthorized act was done on their behalf, rather than from an express statement of approval.
glossary.material knowledge: Full and accurate awareness of the significant facts relevant to a transaction or act, required for a valid ratification.
glossary.transaction: A dealing or set of connected acts between parties, such as a purchase, loan, or sale.
glossary.termination of agency: The ending of an agent's authority to act for the principal, by any of the modes in Sections 201-210.
glossary.renunciation: The act of the agent giving up or abandoning the business of the agency.
glossary.insolvent: A person who is legally adjudicated unable to pay his debts, under the law relating to relief of insolvent debtors.
glossary.agency coupled with interest: An agency in which the agent has his own financial interest in the subject-matter, which as a result cannot be revoked to the agent's prejudice, and does not terminate on the principal's death or unsoundness of mind, absent a contrary contract.
glossary.partly exercised: Describes an agent's authority when it has already been acted upon in part, such that acts and obligations arising from what has been done cannot be undone by later revocation.
glossary.reasonable notice: Notice given within a period of time that is fair and adequate in the circumstances, allowing the other party a genuine opportunity to adjust.
glossary.implied revocation: Revocation of an agent's authority inferred from the principal's conduct, rather than from an express statement.
glossary.knowledge: Actual awareness of a fact — here, of the termination of an agent's authority — which determines when that termination becomes legally effective as against the agent or third persons.
glossary.agency: The legal relationship in which one person (the agent) is empowered to act for, or represent, another person (the principal) in dealings with third parties.
glossary.authority: The power given to an agent, expressly or impliedly, to act on behalf of the principal.
glossary.third persons: Persons who are not parties to the principal-agent relationship itself, but who deal with the agent in the course of the agency's business.
glossary.reasonable steps: The actions a prudent person would take in the circumstances to protect an interest, judged objectively.
glossary.protection and preservation: Steps taken to safeguard property or interests from loss, damage, or deterioration.
glossary.termination of authority: The point at which an agent (or sub-agent) ceases to have the power to bind the principal.
glossary.derivative authority: Authority that exists only because, and to the extent that, another person's (the agent's) authority exists.
glossary.directions: Instructions given by the principal to the agent as to how the agency business is to be conducted.
glossary.custom of trade: The established, generally recognized practice followed in a particular kind of business at a particular place.
glossary.loss sustained: Financial or other detriment suffered as a result of an act or omission.
glossary.profit accrues: A gain or benefit that arises or results from a transaction.
glossary.account for: To report and hand over money or benefit received on another's behalf, rather than keep it.
glossary.reasonable diligence: The degree of care and attention that an ordinarily prudent person would exercise in the circumstances.
glossary.direct consequences: Results that flow immediately and proximately from an act, without an intervening cause.
glossary.remote consequences: Results that are too indirect, speculative, or distant from the act to be legally attributed to it.
glossary.neglect: A failure to exercise the care that a reasonable person would exercise in the circumstances.
glossary.want of skill: A deficiency in the competence or expertise ordinarily expected in a given trade or profession.
glossary.misconduct: Improper, unlawful, or negligent conduct in the performance of one's duties.
glossary.render accounts: To prepare and present a statement of receipts, payments, and dealings.
glossary.on demand: As soon as requested, without need for further notice or delay.
glossary.cases of difficulty: Situations arising during the agency where the agent faces an unexpected problem or uncertainty.
glossary.instructions: Directions given by the principal as to how the agent should act.
glossary.dealing on own account: An agent transacting the business of the agency for his own personal benefit rather than the principal's.
glossary.material circumstances: Facts significant enough that knowledge of them could reasonably affect a party's decision.
glossary.repudiate: To reject or refuse to be bound by a transaction, treating it as not binding.
glossary.dishonestly concealed: Deliberately hidden with an intention to deceive or gain unfair advantage.
glossary.disadvantageous: Resulting in an unfavourable or unfair outcome for a party.
glossary.without knowledge of principal: Occurring without the principal being aware of the act or transaction.
glossary.own account: For one's own benefit, rather than as agent for another.
glossary.claim benefit: To assert a right to receive a gain or advantage obtained by another.
glossary.right of retainer: The right of an agent to deduct and keep sums owed to him before remitting the balance to the principal.
glossary.advances: Sums of money paid out by the agent on the principal's behalf, in anticipation of reimbursement.
glossary.expenses properly incurred: Costs reasonably and legitimately spent by the agent in conducting the agency business.
glossary.remuneration: Payment or reward due to the agent for services rendered as agent.
glossary.deductions: Amounts subtracted from a sum before the remainder is paid over.
glossary.sums received: Money collected or obtained by the agent in the course of the agency business.
glossary.pay to principal: The agent's obligation to remit money collected on the principal's behalf.
glossary.completion of act: The point at which the task the agent was engaged to perform has been fully carried out.
glossary.detain moneys: To hold back and retain money that has been received, pending settlement of what is owed.
glossary.goods consigned: Goods delivered to an agent for the purpose of sale on the principal's behalf.
glossary.remuneration forfeited: The loss of entitlement to payment as a consequence of misconduct.
glossary.apportionment of remuneration: Dividing remuneration between properly performed and improperly performed parts of a task.
glossary.agent's lien: The right of an agent to retain the principal's property in his possession until sums due to him are paid.
glossary.goods, papers and other property: Tangible items, documents, and other assets belonging to the principal that come into the agent's possession.
glossary.commission: A fee payable to an agent, usually calculated as a percentage of the value of business transacted.
glossary.disbursements: Sums of money paid out by the agent on behalf of the principal in the course of the agency.
glossary.contract to the contrary: An agreement between the parties that displaces or varies a default statutory rule.
glossary.lawful acts: Acts that are permitted by, and not contrary to, the law.
glossary.exercise of authority: Acting within the scope of the power conferred by the principal.
glossary.employer of agent: The principal, who engages and directs the agent.
glossary.injury to rights of third persons: Harm caused to the legal rights or interests of a person who is not a party to the agency relationship.
glossary.criminal act: An act that is punishable as an offence under the law.
glossary.non-liability: The absence of a legal obligation to compensate or answer for a consequence.
glossary.injury: Harm or damage suffered by a person, whether physical or otherwise.
glossary.principal's neglect: A failure by the principal to exercise reasonable care, causing harm to the agent.
glossary.enforce contracts: To compel performance of, or claim remedies for breach of, a binding agreement.
glossary.legal consequences: The rights, duties, and liabilities that the law attaches to an act or transaction.
glossary.as if principal in person: Treated in law exactly as though the principal himself had acted, without an intermediary.
glossary.exceeds authority: An agent acting beyond the scope of the power conferred by the principal.
glossary.separable: Capable of being divided into distinct parts that can be treated independently.
glossary.binding: Legally enforceable and imposing an obligation on a party.
glossary.excess of authority: The portion of an agent's act that goes beyond the authority actually conferred.
glossary.not separable: Incapable of being cleanly divided into an authorized part and an unauthorized part.
glossary.repudiate whole transaction: To reject an entire transaction as non-binding, rather than only part of it.
glossary.scope of authority: The boundaries of the power that a principal has conferred on an agent.
glossary.notice to agent: Information or notification communicated to the agent in the course of the agency business.
glossary.imputed knowledge: Knowledge legally attributed to a principal because the agent acquired it in the course of the agency.
glossary.course of business: The ordinary conduct of the transactions that the agent was engaged to carry out.
glossary.third parties: Persons who are not parties to the principal-agent relationship but deal with the agent.
glossary.personally enforce: To sue in one's own right to compel performance of a contract.
glossary.personally bound: Subject to personal liability under a contract, in one's own right.
glossary.presumption of contract to contrary: A legal presumption, in specified situations, that the parties intended to displace the default non-liability rule for agents.
glossary.merchant resident abroad: A trading principal who resides outside the country where the contract is made.
glossary.undisclosed principal: A principal whose existence or identity is not revealed by the agent to the other contracting party.
glossary.principal cannot be sued: A situation where the disclosed principal is, for some legal reason, immune from suit.
glossary.reason to suspect: Circumstances that would put a reasonably attentive person on notice of a fact, even without actual knowledge.
glossary.same rights as against agent: The legal position of the other party is preserved as though the agent, not the principal, were the contracting party.
glossary.refuse to fulfil: To decline to carry out one's obligations under a contract, where legally justified.
glossary.subject to rights and obligations: Bound by, and limited by, the legal rights and duties already existing between other parties.
glossary.set-off: A right to deduct a sum owed by the other party from a sum claimed by them, reducing the net amount payable.
glossary.supposed to be principal: A situation where the other contracting party believes, without cause for suspicion, that they are dealing with a principal, not an agent.
glossary.personally liable: Subject to being sued and held responsible in one's individual capacity.
glossary.hold liable: To pursue a legal claim against a person, making them answerable for an obligation.
glossary.either or both: A choice available to a claimant to proceed against one party, the other, or both together.
glossary.induces belief: Causes another person to form a genuine understanding or expectation through words or conduct.
glossary.exclusively liable: Solely and only responsible, to the exclusion of any other party.
glossary.cannot afterwards hold liable: Barred, typically by estoppel, from later pursuing a claim against a party previously excluded by one's own conduct.
glossary.pretended agent: A person who falsely claims to be the authorized agent of another.
glossary.untruly representing: Making a statement that is false, whether knowingly or not.
glossary.alleged employer: The person whom a pretended agent falsely claims to represent.
glossary.ratify: To adopt and confirm, after the fact, an act done without prior authority, making it binding as though originally authorized.
glossary.falsely contracting as agent: Entering into a contract while claiming to act as an agent, when in reality acting for oneself.
glossary.not entitled to performance: Barred from claiming the other party's performance of a contract.
glossary.without authority: Acting beyond, or without, any power conferred by the principal.
glossary.words or conduct: Statements or behaviour by which a person communicates or represents something to others.
glossary.apparent authority: Authority that a third party reasonably believes an agent possesses, based on the principal's own words or conduct, even if not actually granted.
glossary.induced belief: A conviction or understanding created in another person's mind by words or conduct.
glossary.bound: Legally obligated to honour and perform.
glossary.matters not within authority: Subjects or transactions falling outside the scope of power conferred on the agent.
glossary.voidable: Valid until one party, entitled by law, elects to avoid (cancel) the contract.

sections.title: Short title, extent and commencement
sections.raw_text:
1. Short title.—This Act may be called the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

Extent, Commencement.—It extends to the whole of India; and it shall come into force on the first day of September, 1872.

Saving.—Nothing herein contained shall affect the provisions of any Statute, Act or Regulation not hereby expressly repealed, nor any usage or custom of trade, nor any incident of any contract, not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 1 is the Act's own identity card: it names the statute, fixes its territorial reach (the whole of India), and its commencement date (1 September 1872). The closing "saving" clause is a non-obstante-style protection running the other way — it tells courts this Act is not meant to wipe out other laws, trade customs, or contract-specific incidents unless it expressly says so.
essential_elements: The short title by which the Act is cited is "the Indian Contract Act, 1872".
The Act extends to the whole of India and commenced on 1 September 1872.
Any other Statute, Act or Regulation not expressly repealed by this Act survives untouched.
Trade usages and customs, and incidents of a contract, remain effective so long as they are not inconsistent with the Act.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The saving clause only protects what is not inconsistent with the Act — an express provision of the Contract Act always overrides a conflicting usage or custom.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Section 1 as background, not a live pleading point — it is almost never cited on its own in argument. Its only real practical use is the saving clause: when opposing counsel argues a trade custom or another statute is displaced by the Contract Act, check first whether the Act expressly repeals it or is merely silent, since silence favours the custom/other law surviving.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 1 अधिनियम का अपना परिचय-पत्र है: यह क़ानून का नाम बताती है, इसका क्षेत्रीय विस्तार (संपूर्ण भारत) तय करती है, और इसके प्रवर्तन की तिथि (1 सितंबर 1872) निर्धारित करती है। अंतिम 'बचत' खंड एक विपरीत दिशा में काम करने वाला संरक्षण है — यह न्यायालयों को बताता है कि यह अधिनियम अन्य कानूनों, व्यापारिक रूढ़ियों, या संविदा-विशिष्ट प्रसंगों को समाप्त करने के लिए नहीं बना है, जब तक कि यह स्पष्ट रूप से ऐसा न कहे।
essential_elements_hi: इस अधिनियम का संक्षिप्त नाम 'भारतीय संविदा अधिनियम, 1872' है।
यह अधिनियम संपूर्ण भारत पर लागू होता है और 1 सितंबर 1872 को प्रवृत्त हुआ।
इस अधिनियम द्वारा स्पष्ट रूप से निरसित न किया गया कोई अन्य कानून, अधिनियम या विनियम अप्रभावित बना रहता है।
व्यापारिक रूढ़ियाँ और प्रथाएँ, तथा किसी संविदा के प्रसंग, तब तक प्रभावी बने रहते हैं जब तक वे अधिनियम के विपरीत न हों।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: बचत खंड केवल उसी को संरक्षित करता है जो अधिनियम के विपरीत न हो — संविदा अधिनियम का कोई स्पष्ट प्रावधान सदैव किसी परस्पर-विरोधी प्रथा या रूढ़ि पर अधिभावी होता है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 1 को पृष्ठभूमि के रूप में लें, न कि किसी सजीव वाद-बिंदु के रूप में — यह लगभग कभी भी अकेले तर्क में उद्धृत नहीं की जाती। इसका एकमात्र व्यावहारिक उपयोग बचत खंड है: जब विरोधी पक्ष का वकील यह तर्क दे कि कोई व्यापारिक प्रथा या अन्य कानून संविदा अधिनियम द्वारा विस्थापित हो गया है, तो पहले यह जाँचें कि क्या अधिनियम उसे स्पष्ट रूप से निरसित करता है या मात्र मौन है, क्योंकि मौन प्रथा/अन्य कानून के बने रहने के पक्ष में जाता है।

sections.title: Interpretation-clause

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 2 is the Act's dictionary — every other section relies on these ten defined terms. It builds a chain: a proposal (offer) that is accepted becomes a promise; a promise (or set of promises) forming consideration for each other is an agreement; and an agreement enforceable by law is a contract. It also separately defines the two defective categories — void (never enforceable) and voidable (enforceable only at one party's option).
essential_elements: Proposal (offer): a signified willingness to do or abstain from something, aimed at obtaining another's assent.
Acceptance: the offeree's signified assent to the proposal, which converts it into a promise.
Consideration: something done, not done, or promised at the desire of the promisor, by the promisee or any other person.
Agreement: every promise, or set of reciprocal promises, forming the consideration for each other.
Void agreement: one not enforceable by law at all.
Contract: an agreement enforceable by law.
Voidable contract: enforceable at the option of one or more parties, but not the other(s).
exceptions_and_qualifications: These definitions apply "unless a contrary intention appears from the context" — a contextual reading can displace the literal definition in an unusual case.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 2 is a lookup table, not a rule of decision — pleadings should cite it only to anchor terminology, then move to the operative section (e.g. Section 10 for contract formation, Section 2(g)/(j) alongside Sections 24-30 for void agreements). Note the deliberate distinction between clause (g) "void" and clause (i) "voidable": a void agreement was never enforceable, while a voidable contract was enforceable until the aggrieved party elects to avoid it — conflating the two is a common and costly drafting error.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 2 अधिनियम का शब्दकोश है — बाकी हर धारा इन दस परिभाषित शब्दों पर निर्भर करती है। यह एक शृंखला बनाती है: स्वीकृत प्रस्ताव वचन (promise) बन जाता है; परस्पर एक-दूसरे के लिए प्रतिफल बनने वाला वचन (या वचन-समूह) करार (agreement) है; और विधितः प्रवर्तनीय करार संविदा (contract) है। यह दो दोषपूर्ण श्रेणियों — शून्य (कभी प्रवर्तनीय नहीं) और शून्यकरणीय (केवल एक पक्ष के विकल्प पर प्रवर्तनीय) — को भी अलग से परिभाषित करती है।
essential_elements_hi: प्रस्ताव: किसी बात को करने या न करने की इच्छा का संसूचन, जिसका उद्देश्य दूसरे की सहमति प्राप्त करना हो।
स्वीकृति: प्रस्ताव-प्राप्तकर्ता द्वारा प्रस्ताव के प्रति संसूचित सहमति, जो उसे वचन में बदल देती है।
प्रतिफल: वचनदाता की इच्छा पर, वचनगृहीता या किसी अन्य व्यक्ति द्वारा किया गया, न किया गया, या किए जाने का वचन दिया गया कोई कार्य।
करार: हर वचन, या परस्पर वचनों का समूह, जो एक-दूसरे के लिए प्रतिफल बनाते हैं।
शून्य करार: वह जो विधितः बिल्कुल भी प्रवर्तनीय न हो।
संविदा: विधितः प्रवर्तनीय करार।
शून्यकरणीय संविदा: एक या अधिक पक्षों के विकल्प पर प्रवर्तनीय, परंतु अन्य पक्ष(षों) के विकल्प पर नहीं।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: ये परिभाषाएँ तभी तक लागू होती हैं 'जब तक प्रसंग से विपरीत आशय प्रकट न हो' — असामान्य मामलों में प्रासंगिक पठन शाब्दिक परिभाषा को विस्थापित कर सकता है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 2 एक संदर्भ-सूची है, निर्णय का नियम नहीं — वाद-पत्रों में इसे केवल शब्दावली स्थिर करने हेतु उद्धृत करें, फिर संबंधित प्रावधान (जैसे संविदा-निर्माण हेतु धारा 10, शून्य करारों हेतु धारा 24-30) की ओर बढ़ें। 'शून्य' और 'शून्यकरणीय' के बीच जानबूझकर किए गए भेद पर ध्यान दें: शून्य करार कभी प्रवर्तनीय नहीं था, जबकि शून्यकरणीय संविदा तब तक प्रवर्तनीय थी जब तक पीड़ित पक्ष उसे शून्य करने का विकल्प नहीं चुनता — इन दोनों को गड्डमड्ड करना एक सामान्य और महँगी प्रारूपण त्रुटि है।

sections.title: Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals
sections.raw_text: 3. Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals.—The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 3 defines how communication itself happens for the purposes of proposals, acceptances, and revocations. It is deliberately broad: any act or omission that either is intended to communicate, or actually has the effect of communicating, counts — conduct (not just words) can communicate a proposal, an acceptance, or a revocation.
essential_elements: Communication can occur by act or by omission (silence in context can, exceptionally, communicate).
Intent to communicate is one sufficient route.
Even without intent, an act that has the effect of communicating still counts.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 3 is the general mechanism provision; Section 4 then supplies the precise moment each type of communication is treated as "complete". Always read the two together — Section 3 answers "does this count as communication at all", Section 4 answers "and if so, exactly when did it take legal effect".
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 3 यह परिभाषित करती है कि प्रस्तावों, स्वीकृतियों, और प्रतिसंहरणों (revocations) के प्रयोजन के लिए संचार (communication) स्वयं कैसे होता है। यह जानबूझकर व्यापक है: कोई भी कार्य या लोप, चाहे वह संचार के आशय से हो या वास्तव में संचार का प्रभाव रखता हो, मान्य होता है — आचरण (केवल शब्द नहीं) भी प्रस्ताव, स्वीकृति, या प्रतिसंहरण का संचार कर सकता है।
essential_elements_hi: संचार कार्य द्वारा या लोप द्वारा हो सकता है (संदर्भ में मौन भी, अपवादस्वरूप, संचार कर सकता है)।
संचार का आशय एक पर्याप्त मार्ग है।
आशय के बिना भी, यदि किसी कार्य का प्रभाव संचार करना हो, तो वह मान्य होता है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 3 सामान्य प्रक्रिया-प्रावधान है; धारा 4 फिर प्रत्येक प्रकार के संचार के 'पूर्ण' माने जाने के ठीक क्षण को निर्धारित करती है। दोनों को सदैव साथ पढ़ें — धारा 3 यह उत्तर देती है 'क्या यह संचार माना जाएगा', धारा 4 यह उत्तर देती है 'और यदि हाँ, तो यह ठीक कब विधिक रूप से प्रभावी हुआ'।

sections.title: Communication when complete
sections.raw_text:
4. Communication when complete.—The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made.

The communication of an acceptance is complete,—
as against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor;
as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.

The communication of a revocation is complete,—
as against the person who makes it, when it is put into a course of transmission to the person to whom it is made, so as to be out of the power of the person who makes it;
as against the person to whom it is made, when it comes to his knowledge.

Illustrations

(a) A proposes, by letter, to sell a house to B at a certain price. The communication of the proposal is complete when B receives the letter.

(b) B accepts A's proposal by a letter sent by post. The communication of the acceptance is complete, as against A when the letter is posted; as against B, when the letter is received by A.

(c) A revokes his proposal by telegram. The revocation is complete as against A when the telegram is despatched. It is complete as against B when B receives it. B revokes his acceptance by telegram. B's revocation is complete as against B when the telegram is despatched, and as against A when it reaches him.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 4 pins down the exact moment at which a proposal, an acceptance, and a revocation each become legally complete — and, critically, an acceptance is complete against the two parties at two different moments. This asymmetry (the famous "postal rule") is what lets Section 5 fix the window during which a proposal or an acceptance can still be revoked.
essential_elements: A proposal is complete only when it reaches the knowledge of the offeree.
An acceptance is complete against the proposer the moment it is posted/transmitted (out of the acceptor's power) — the proposer is bound from that instant even before he learns of it.
An acceptance is complete against the acceptor only when it actually reaches the proposer's knowledge.
A revocation follows the same two-stage pattern: complete against its sender on transmission, complete against its recipient only on receipt.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the classic examination and drafting trap: because acceptance binds the proposer on posting but binds the acceptor only on receipt, there is a window (between posting and delivery) where the proposer is bound but the acceptor is not yet — during which only the acceptor, not the proposer, can still revoke. Always work out separately "complete as against whom" before answering any fact pattern involving post, telegram, or electronic transmission delays.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 4 उस ठीक क्षण को निर्धारित करती है जिस पर प्रस्ताव, स्वीकृति, और प्रतिसंहरण प्रत्येक विधितः पूर्ण माने जाते हैं — और, सबसे महत्वपूर्ण बात, एक स्वीकृति दोनों पक्षों के विरुद्ध दो अलग-अलग क्षणों पर पूर्ण मानी जाती है। यही असमानता (प्रसिद्ध 'डाक नियम') धारा 5 को वह अवधि तय करने देती है जिसके दौरान प्रस्ताव या स्वीकृति अभी भी प्रतिसंहृत की जा सकती है।
essential_elements_hi: प्रस्ताव तभी पूर्ण माना जाता है जब वह प्रस्ताव-प्राप्तकर्ता के ज्ञान में आ जाए।

स्वीकृति प्रस्तावक के विरुद्ध उसी क्षण पूर्ण मानी जाती है जब वह डाक में डाली/प्रेषित की जाती है (स्वीकर्ता के नियंत्रण से बाहर हो जाती है) — प्रस्तावक उसी क्षण से बाध्य हो जाता है, भले ही उसे इसकी जानकारी बाद में मिले।
स्वीकृति स्वीकर्ता के विरुद्ध तभी पूर्ण मानी जाती है जब वह वास्तव में प्रस्तावक के ज्ञान में आ जाए।
प्रतिसंहरण भी इसी दो-चरणीय प्रतिमान का पालन करता है: प्रेषक के विरुद्ध प्रेषण पर पूर्ण, प्राप्तकर्ता के विरुद्ध केवल प्राप्ति पर पूर्ण।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: यह एक प्रसिद्ध परीक्षा एवं प्रारूपण जाल है: चूँकि स्वीकृति डाक में डालने पर प्रस्तावक को बाध्य करती है परंतु स्वीकर्ता को केवल प्राप्ति पर बाध्य करती है, इसलिए एक ऐसी अवधि होती है जिसमें प्रस्तावक बाध्य है परंतु स्वीकर्ता अभी नहीं — जिसके दौरान केवल स्वीकर्ता, प्रस्तावक नहीं, प्रतिसंहरण कर सकता है। डाक, तार, या इलेक्ट्रॉनिक प्रेषण विलंब से जुड़े किसी भी तथ्य-प्रतिमान का उत्तर देने से पहले सदैव अलग-अलग निकालें कि 'किसके विरुद्ध पूर्ण' है।

sections.title: Revocation of proposals and acceptances
sections.raw_text:
5. Revocation of proposals and acceptances.—A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards.

An acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.

Illustration

A proposes, by a letter sent by post, to sell his house to B. B accepts the proposal by a letter sent by post. A may revoke his proposal at any time before or at the moment when B posts his letter of acceptance, but not afterwards. B may revoke his acceptance at any time before or at the moment when the letter communicating it reaches A, but not afterwards.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 5 sets the deadline for revoking a proposal and for revoking an acceptance, by cross-referring to the two different "complete" moments fixed in Section 4. A proposer's right to revoke dies the instant the acceptor posts acceptance; an acceptor's right to revoke survives a little longer — until the acceptance actually reaches the proposer.
essential_elements: A proposal can be revoked only up to the moment acceptance is posted/put in a course of transmission by the acceptor — not after.
An acceptance can be revoked only up to the moment it actually reaches the proposer — even though it may already be in transit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: State amendments exist for this section in some States (e.g. Uttar Pradesh has inserted a proviso deeming certain time-bound offers irrevocable) — always check the applicable State amendment before advising on revocation timing outside the central Act.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair Section 5 directly with Section 4's illustrations — the deadline language ("before... complete as against") only makes sense once you have already fixed the two separate completion moments. In practice this section decides last-minute telegram/email revocation disputes: the question is always whether the revocation reached its target before the relevant completion moment for the proposal or acceptance it seeks to undo.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 5, धारा 4 में तय किए गए दो अलग-अलग 'पूर्ण' क्षणों का संदर्भ देते हुए, प्रस्ताव के प्रतिसंहरण और स्वीकृति के प्रतिसंहरण के लिए समय-सीमा निर्धारित करती है। प्रस्तावक का प्रतिसंहरण का अधिकार उसी क्षण समाप्त हो जाता है जब स्वीकर्ता स्वीकृति डाक में डालता है; स्वीकर्ता का प्रतिसंहरण का अधिकार थोड़ा अधिक समय तक — जब तक स्वीकृति वास्तव में प्रस्तावक तक नहीं पहुँच जाती — बना रहता है।
essential_elements_hi: प्रस्ताव का प्रतिसंहरण केवल उस क्षण तक किया जा सकता है जब स्वीकर्ता स्वीकृति डाक में डाले/प्रेषण-क्रम में रखे — उसके बाद नहीं।
स्वीकृति का प्रतिसंहरण केवल उस क्षण तक किया जा सकता है जब वह वास्तव में प्रस्तावक तक पहुँचे — भले ही वह पहले से ही मार्ग में हो।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: कुछ राज्यों में इस धारा हेतु राज्य संशोधन विद्यमान हैं (उदाहरणतः उत्तर प्रदेश ने एक परंतुक जोड़ा है जो कुछ समय-सीमित प्रस्तावों को अप्रतिसंहरणीय मानता है) — केंद्रीय अधिनियम से बाहर प्रतिसंहरण के समय पर सलाह देने से पहले सदैव लागू राज्य संशोधन जाँच लें।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 5 को सीधे धारा 4 के उदाहरणों के साथ जोड़ें — समय-सीमा की भाषा तभी समझ में आती है जब आपने पहले ही दोनों अलग-अलग पूर्णता-क्षण तय कर लिए हों। व्यवहार में यह धारा अंतिम-क्षण के तार/ईमेल प्रतिसंहरण विवादों का निर्णय करती है: प्रश्न सदैव यह होता है कि क्या प्रतिसंहरण उस प्रस्ताव या स्वीकृति, जिसे वह निष्प्रभावी करना चाहता है, के लिए प्रासंगिक पूर्णता-क्षण से पहले अपने लक्ष्य तक पहुँचा।

sections.title: Revocation, how made

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 6 lists the four exhaustive ways a proposal comes to an end by revocation: an express notice, expiry of a stated or reasonable time, non-fulfilment of a condition precedent to acceptance, or the proposer's death/insanity (but only if the acceptor knows of it before accepting).
essential_elements: Express notice of revocation communicated to the offeree.
Lapse of the time fixed in the proposal for acceptance (or a reasonable time, if none is fixed).
Failure of the acceptor to satisfy any condition precedent attached to acceptance.
Death or insanity of the proposer — but only revokes the proposal if the acceptor learns of it before accepting.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the acceptor accepts without knowledge of the proposer's death or insanity, the acceptance can still validly complete the contract — clause (4) only bars acceptance made with knowledge.
breakdown.how_to_read: "Reasonable time" under clause (2) is a question of fact, not a fixed period — assess it against the subject matter (perishable goods vs. real estate) and the mode of communication used. Clause (4) is a frequent examination trap: the death/insanity revokes the offer only prospectively from the acceptor's knowledge, so a valid acceptance made in ignorance of the proposer's death can still bind the estate.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 6 उन चार संपूर्ण तरीकों को सूचीबद्ध करती है जिनसे प्रतिसंहरण द्वारा कोई प्रस्ताव समाप्त होता है: स्पष्ट सूचना, निर्धारित या युक्तियुक्त समय की समाप्ति, स्वीकृति के लिए पूर्व-शर्त की अपूर्ति, या प्रस्तावक की मृत्यु/उन्मत्तता (परंतु केवल तभी जब स्वीकर्ता को स्वीकृति देने से पहले इसकी जानकारी हो)।
essential_elements_hi: प्रस्ताव-प्राप्तकर्ता को संसूचित प्रतिसंहरण की स्पष्ट सूचना।
प्रस्ताव में स्वीकृति हेतु निर्धारित समय की समाप्ति (या, यदि कोई समय निर्धारित न हो, युक्तियुक्त समय की समाप्ति)।
स्वीकृति से संलग्न किसी पूर्व-शर्त को पूरा करने में स्वीकर्ता की विफलता।
प्रस्तावक की मृत्यु या उन्मत्तता — परंतु यह प्रस्ताव को केवल तभी प्रतिसंहृत करती है जब स्वीकर्ता को स्वीकृति देने से पहले इसका पता चल जाए।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: यदि स्वीकर्ता प्रस्तावक की मृत्यु या उन्मत्तता की जानकारी के बिना स्वीकृति देता है, तो वह स्वीकृति अब भी संविदा को वैध रूप से पूर्ण कर सकती है — खंड (4) केवल जानकारी सहित दी गई स्वीकृति को रोकता है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: खंड (2) के अंतर्गत 'युक्तियुक्त समय' एक तथ्य का प्रश्न है, निश्चित अवधि नहीं — इसका आकलन विषय-वस्तु (नाशवान वस्तुएँ बनाम स्थावर संपत्ति) और उपयोग किए गए संचार-माध्यम के आधार पर करें। खंड (4) एक सामान्य परीक्षा-जाल है: मृत्यु/उन्मत्तता प्रस्ताव को केवल स्वीकर्ता की जानकारी से आगे की ओर प्रतिसंहृत करती है, अतः प्रस्तावक की मृत्यु से अनभिज्ञ रहते हुए दी गई वैध स्वीकृति अब भी संपदा को बाध्य कर सकती है।

sections.title: Acceptance must be absolute

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 7 lays down the two conditions an acceptance must meet to actually convert a proposal into a binding promise: it must mirror the proposal exactly (absolute and unqualified — a qualified "acceptance" is really a counter-proposal), and it must be communicated in a reasonable manner, or in whatever manner the proposal specifically demanded.
essential_elements: The acceptance must match the proposal exactly, with no variation, condition, or addition (the "mirror image" rule).
Absent a prescribed manner, acceptance must be communicated in some usual and reasonable way given the circumstances.
If the proposal prescribes a manner and the offeree departs from it, the proposer must object within a reasonable time or is deemed to have accepted the acceptance as given.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proposer's failure to promptly object to a non-prescribed mode of acceptance operates as a waiver — silence beyond a reasonable time cures the defect.
breakdown.how_to_read: A "qualified" or conditional acceptance is not an acceptance at all under this section — it is a fresh proposal (a counter-offer) that itself now requires acceptance by the original proposer to form a contract. Plead departures from a prescribed acceptance mode carefully: the proposer must show he objected promptly, or the acceptance stands despite the departure.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 7 उन दो शर्तों को निर्धारित करती है जो किसी स्वीकृति को वास्तव में प्रस्ताव को बाध्यकारी वचन में बदलने के लिए पूरी करनी होती हैं: उसे प्रस्ताव को बिल्कुल प्रतिबिंबित करना चाहिए (पूर्ण और अशर्त — एक शर्तयुक्त 'स्वीकृति' वास्तव में एक प्रति-प्रस्ताव है), और उसे युक्तियुक्त रीति से, या प्रस्ताव द्वारा विशेष रूप से माँगी गई किसी भी रीति से, संसूचित किया जाना चाहिए।
essential_elements_hi: स्वीकृति को प्रस्ताव से बिल्कुल मेल खाना चाहिए, बिना किसी परिवर्तन, शर्त, या अतिरिक्त के ('दर्पण-प्रतिबिंब' नियम)।
यदि कोई निर्धारित रीति न हो, तो परिस्थितियों के अनुसार किसी सामान्य और युक्तियुक्त रीति से स्वीकृति संसूचित होनी चाहिए।
यदि प्रस्ताव कोई रीति निर्धारित करता है और प्रस्ताव-प्राप्तकर्ता उससे विचलित होता है, तो प्रस्तावक को युक्तियुक्त समय के भीतर आपत्ति करनी होगी, अन्यथा वह दी गई स्वीकृति को स्वीकार कर चुका माना जाएगा।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: निर्धारित रीति से भिन्न स्वीकृति पर प्रस्तावक की तुरंत आपत्ति न करना परित्याग के रूप में कार्य करता है — युक्तियुक्त समय से अधिक मौन त्रुटि को दूर कर देता है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: एक 'शर्तयुक्त' या सशर्त स्वीकृति इस धारा के अंतर्गत बिल्कुल भी स्वीकृति नहीं है — यह एक नया प्रस्ताव (प्रति-प्रस्ताव) है जिसे अब मूल प्रस्तावक द्वारा संविदा बनाने हेतु स्वीकार किया जाना आवश्यक है। निर्धारित स्वीकृति-रीति से विचलन का तर्क सावधानी से प्रस्तुत करें: प्रस्तावक को यह दिखाना होगा कि उसने तुरंत आपत्ति की, अन्यथा विचलन के बावजूद स्वीकृति कायम रहती है।

sections.title: Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration
sections.raw_text: 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration.—Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 8 recognises that acceptance need not be a spoken or written "yes" — conduct itself can be an acceptance. Doing what the proposal asked for, or taking the benefit offered along with a reciprocal promise, counts as accepting the proposal without any separate communication of assent.
essential_elements: Performing the exact conditions stipulated in the proposal amounts to acceptance (e.g. a reward-for-return-of-lost-property offer accepted by actually returning the property).
Accepting consideration offered alongside a reciprocal promise likewise operates as acceptance.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 8 is the statutory basis for "unilateral contract" fact patterns (reward notices, general offers to the public) — the classic Carlill-style problem. Plead performance of the stipulated act itself as the acceptance; there is no additional need to separately notify the offeror of assent before performing.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 8 यह मानती है कि स्वीकृति कोई बोला या लिखा हुआ 'हाँ' होना आवश्यक नहीं — आचरण स्वयं स्वीकृति हो सकता है। प्रस्ताव में माँगी गई बात करना, या प्रतिदेय वचन के साथ दिए गए लाभ को लेना, बिना किसी अलग सहमति-संसूचन के प्रस्ताव को स्वीकार करना माना जाता है।
essential_elements_hi: प्रस्ताव में निर्धारित ठीक शर्तों का पालन करना स्वीकृति के बराबर है (उदाहरणतः खोई हुई संपत्ति लौटाने पर पुरस्कार का प्रस्ताव, संपत्ति वास्तव में लौटाकर स्वीकार किया जाना)।
प्रतिदेय वचन के साथ प्रस्तावित प्रतिफल को स्वीकार करना भी स्वीकृति के रूप में कार्य करता है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 8 'एकपक्षीय संविदा' तथ्य-प्रतिमानों (पुरस्कार-सूचनाएँ, जनता को सामान्य प्रस्ताव) का वैधानिक आधार है — प्रसिद्ध कार्लिल-शैली की समस्या। निर्धारित कार्य के वास्तविक पालन को ही स्वीकृति के रूप में प्रस्तुत करें; पालन करने से पहले प्रस्तावक को सहमति की अलग से सूचना देने की कोई अतिरिक्त आवश्यकता नहीं है।

sections.title: Promises, express and implied
sections.raw_text: 9. Promises, express and implied.—In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 9 draws the line between an express promise (made in words, spoken or written) and an implied promise (inferred from conduct, without words). Both are equally valid ways of proposing or accepting — the Act does not privilege one form over the other.
essential_elements: A promise made in words (oral or written) is express.
A promise inferred from conduct, without words, is implied.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use Section 9 whenever a party denies any contract exists purely because nothing was written or spoken — conduct (boarding a bus, ordering at a restaurant, continuing to accept deliveries) can itself constitute a proposal or acceptance under this section, forming an implied contract with the same legal force as an express one.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 9 स्पष्ट वचन (शब्दों में, बोला या लिखा हुआ) और विवक्षित वचन (आचरण से, बिना शब्दों के, अनुमानित) के बीच रेखा खींचती है। प्रस्ताव करने या स्वीकार करने के दोनों तरीके समान रूप से मान्य हैं — अधिनियम किसी एक रूप को दूसरे पर वरीयता नहीं देता।
essential_elements_hi: शब्दों में (मौखिक या लिखित) दिया गया वचन स्पष्ट (express) है।
बिना शब्दों के, आचरण से अनुमानित वचन विवक्षित (implied) है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 9 का उपयोग तब करें जब कोई पक्ष केवल इसलिए किसी संविदा के अस्तित्व से इनकार करे कि कुछ भी लिखा या बोला नहीं गया — आचरण (बस में चढ़ना, रेस्तरां में ऑर्डर देना, वितरण स्वीकार करना जारी रखना) स्वयं इस धारा के अंतर्गत प्रस्ताव या स्वीकृति का गठन कर सकता है, जो स्पष्ट संविदा के समान ही विधिक बल रखने वाली विवक्षित संविदा बनाती है।

sections.title: What agreements are contracts
sections.raw_text:
10. What agreements are contracts.—All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in India and not hereby expressly repealed, by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 10 is the master checklist for turning a plain agreement into a legally enforceable contract. An agreement becomes a contract only when five conditions are satisfied together: free consent, competent parties, lawful consideration, a lawful object, and the agreement is not one that the Act itself declares void.
essential_elements: There must be an agreement between two or more parties (offer + acceptance).
Consent must be free — not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake (Section 14).
All parties must be competent to contract under Section 11 (age of majority, sound mind, not disqualified by law).
There must be lawful consideration flowing between the parties.
The object of the agreement must be lawful.
The agreement must not fall into any category expressly declared void elsewhere in the Act (e.g. Sections 24-30).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The second paragraph is a savings clause: it does not create new formality requirements, but preserves any existing Indian law that requires a particular contract to be in writing, attested by witnesses, or registered (e.g. gift deeds, certain leases under the Transfer of Property Act, or the Registration Act, 1908).

Section 10 does not itself require writing or registration for a contract to be valid — oral contracts are generally enforceable unless another statute says otherwise for that specific type of transaction.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Section 10 as the general validity test, then cross-refer outward: 'free consent' sends you to Section 14, 'competent to contract' sends you to Section 11, and 'not expressly declared void' sends you to the specific void-agreement provisions (Sections 20, 23-30, 56). Section 10 rarely operates alone in argument — it is almost always pleaded together with the specific section that the opposing side is alleged to have breached.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 10 यह बताती है कि एक साधारण करार (agreement) कब कानूनी रूप से बाध्यकारी संविदा (contract) बन जाता है। कोई करार तभी संविदा बनता है जब पाँचों शर्तें एक साथ पूरी हों: पक्षों की स्वतंत्र सहमति, संविदा करने में सक्षम पक्ष, वैध प्रतिफल, वैध उद्देश्य, और वह करार इस अधिनियम द्वारा स्पष्ट रूप से शून्य घोषित न किया गया हो।
essential_elements_hi: दो या अधिक पक्षों के बीच एक करार होना चाहिए (प्रस्ताव + स्वीकृति)।
सहमति स्वतंत्र होनी चाहिए — प्रपीड़न, असम्यक असर, कपट, मिथ्या-व्यपदेशन, या भूल से प्रभावित न हो (धारा 14)।
सभी पक्ष धारा 11 के अंतर्गत संविदा करने में सक्षम होने चाहिए (वयस्कता की आयु, स्वस्थ मस्तिष्क, और कानून द्वारा अयोग्य घोषित न होना)।
पक्षों के बीच वैध प्रतिफल (consideration) का आदान-प्रदान होना चाहिए।
करार का उद्देश्य वैध होना चाहिए।
करार अधिनियम में अन्यत्र स्पष्ट रूप से शून्य घोषित किसी श्रेणी में नहीं आना चाहिए (जैसे धारा 24-30)।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: दूसरा अनुच्छेद एक बचत खंड (savings clause) है: यह कोई नई औपचारिकता की आवश्यकता पैदा नहीं करता, बल्कि किसी भी विद्यमान भारतीय कानून को सुरक्षित रखता है जो किसी विशेष प्रकार की संविदा को लिखित रूप में, साक्षियों द्वारा सत्यापित, या पंजीकृत कराए जाने की माँग करता हो (जैसे दान-पत्र, संपत्ति अंतरण अधिनियम के अंतर्गत कुछ पट्टे, या पंजीकरण अधिनियम, 1908)।
धारा 10 स्वयं किसी संविदा की वैधता के लिए लेखन या पंजीकरण अनिवार्य नहीं करती — जब तक कोई अन्य कानून किसी विशेष प्रकार के लेन-देन के लिए अलग से न कहे, मौखिक संविदाएँ सामान्यतः प्रवर्तनीय होती हैं।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 10 को सामान्य वैधता-परीक्षण के रूप में पढ़ें, फिर संबंधित धाराओं की ओर जाएँ: 'स्वतंत्र सहमति' के लिए धारा 14 देखें, 'संविदा करने में सक्षम' के लिए धारा 11 देखें, और 'स्पष्ट रूप से शून्य घोषित नहीं' के लिए विशिष्ट शून्य-करार प्रावधान (धारा 20, 23-30, 56) देखें। व्यवहार में धारा 10 अकेले शायद ही कभी तर्क में प्रयोग होती है — इसे प्रायः उस विशिष्ट धारा के साथ जोड़कर प्रस्तुत किया जाता है जिसके उल्लंघन का आरोप विरोधी पक्ष पर लगाया गया है।

sections.title: Who are competent to contract
sections.raw_text: 11. Who are competent to contract.—Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 11 defines exactly who is legally allowed to enter into a binding contract. A person qualifies only if they satisfy all three tests: they have reached adulthood under the law that applies to them, they are mentally capable of understanding the deal, and no other law specifically bars them from contracting.
essential_elements: Age of majority: ordinarily 18 years under the Indian Majority Act, 1875 (21 years where a court-appointed guardian manages the minor's person or property).
Soundness of mind: the person must, at the time of contracting, satisfy the Section 12 test.
No legal disqualification: the person must not be barred from contracting by any other applicable law (e.g. certain restrictions on alien enemies, insolvents, or convicts under specific statutes).
exceptions_and_qualifications: A minor's agreement is not merely voidable — it is void ab initio (settled by Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose), which is a stronger consequence than the ordinary voidability rules that apply to other incompetent persons.
Persons of unsound mind can still contract during lucid intervals — incapacity is assessed at the moment of the transaction, not as a permanent status (see Section 12).
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 11 is a three-part conjunctive test — all three limbs (age, mind, no disqualification) must be met; failing any one limb makes the party incompetent. When drafting a plaint or defence, always plead competency as of the date the contract was made, not the date of the suit.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 11 यह स्पष्ट करती है कि कानूनी रूप से बाध्यकारी संविदा में प्रवेश करने का अधिकार वास्तव में किसे है। कोई व्यक्ति तभी योग्य माना जाता है जब वह तीनों परीक्षाओं को पूरा करे: वह उस कानून के अनुसार वयस्क हो जो उस पर लागू होता है, वह मानसिक रूप से सौदे को समझने में सक्षम हो, और कोई अन्य कानून उसे संविदा करने से विशेष रूप से प्रतिबंधित न करता हो।
essential_elements_hi: वयस्कता की आयु: सामान्यतः भारतीय वयस्कता अधिनियम, 1875 के अंतर्गत 18 वर्ष (जहाँ न्यायालय द्वारा नियुक्त संरक्षक नाबालिग के व्यक्ति या संपत्ति का प्रबंधन करता है, वहाँ 21 वर्ष)।
स्वस्थ मस्तिष्क: संविदा के समय व्यक्ति को धारा 12 की कसौटी पूरी करनी चाहिए।
कोई कानूनी अयोग्यता नहीं: व्यक्ति किसी अन्य लागू कानून द्वारा संविदा करने से प्रतिबंधित न हो (जैसे कुछ विशेष कानूनों के अंतर्गत शत्रु-विदेशी, दिवालिया, या दोषसिद्ध व्यक्तियों पर प्रतिबंध)।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: नाबालिग का करार केवल शून्यकरणीय (voidable) नहीं, बल्कि आरंभ से ही शून्य (void ab initio) होता है — यह मोहरी बीबी बनाम धर्मोदास घोष वाद में स्थापित सिद्धांत है, जो अन्य अयोग्य व्यक्तियों पर लागू सामान्य शून्यकरणीयता के नियमों से अधिक कठोर परिणाम है।

अस्वस्थ मस्तिष्क वाले व्यक्ति भी स्वस्थ अंतराल (lucid interval) के दौरान वैध संविदा कर सकते हैं — अक्षमता का आकलन लेन-देन के ठीक उसी क्षण किया जाता है, न कि किसी स्थायी स्थिति के आधार पर (धारा 12 देखें)।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 11 एक त्रि-स्तरीय संयुक्त परीक्षण है — तीनों शर्तें (आयु, मस्तिष्क, कोई अयोग्यता नहीं) पूरी होनी चाहिए; किसी एक भी शर्त के विफल होने पर पक्ष अयोग्य माना जाएगा। वाद-पत्र या प्रतिवाद तैयार करते समय, सक्षमता का दावा सदैव संविदा बनने की तिथि के अनुसार करें, वाद दायर करने की तिथि के अनुसार नहीं।

sections.title: What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting
sections.raw_text:
12. What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting.—A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.

A person who is usually of unsound mind, but occasionally of sound mind, may make a contract when he is of sound mind.

A person who is usually of sound mind, but occasionally of unsound mind, may not make a contract when he is of unsound mind.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 12 supplies the working test for 'sound mind' referenced in Section 11. It is a functional, moment-in-time test — not a diagnostic or permanent label. What matters is whether the person, at the exact moment they signed or agreed, could understand the contract's terms and judge how it would affect their own interests.
essential_elements: Capacity to understand the terms of the contract itself.
Capacity to form a rational judgment about how the contract affects one's own interests.
Both capacities must exist at the precise time the contract is made — not before or after.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A person usually of unsound mind (e.g. someone with a diagnosed mental illness) can validly contract during a lucid interval when they meet the test.
A person usually of sound mind cannot validly contract during a temporary episode of unsoundness (e.g. delirium, severe intoxication, or a psychotic episode) even if that episode is brief.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 12 should always be read together with Section 11 — Section 11 says sound mind is required, Section 12 defines it. In court, the burden typically falls on the party alleging unsoundness to prove incapacity existed specifically at the moment of contracting; medical evidence about the person's general condition is relevant but not conclusive by itself.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 12, धारा 11 में उल्लिखित 'स्वस्थ मस्तिष्क' की व्यावहारिक कसौटी प्रदान करती है। यह एक कार्यात्मक, क्षण-विशेष पर आधारित परीक्षण है — कोई स्थायी या चिकित्सकीय लेबल नहीं। महत्वपूर्ण यह है कि व्यक्ति, जिस ठीक क्षण उसने हस्ताक्षर किए या सहमति दी, क्या वह संविदा की शर्तों को समझने और अपने हितों पर उसके प्रभाव का तर्कसंगत निर्णय लेने में सक्षम था।
essential_elements_hi: संविदा की शर्तों को समझने की क्षमता।
संविदा अपने हितों को कैसे प्रभावित करेगी, इस बारे में तर्कसंगत निर्णय लेने की क्षमता।
दोनों क्षमताएँ ठीक उसी समय विद्यमान होनी चाहिए जब संविदा बनाई जाती है — न उससे पहले, न उसके बाद।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: सामान्यतः अस्वस्थ मस्तिष्क वाला व्यक्ति (जैसे किसी निदानित मानसिक बीमारी से ग्रस्त व्यक्ति) स्वस्थ अंतराल के दौरान वैध संविदा कर सकता है, बशर्ते वह उस समय परीक्षण की शर्तें पूरी करे।
सामान्यतः स्वस्थ मस्तिष्क वाला व्यक्ति अस्वस्थता के किसी अस्थायी प्रकरण (जैसे प्रलाप, गंभीर नशा, या मनोविकृति का दौरा) के दौरान वैध संविदा नहीं कर सकता, भले ही वह प्रकरण अल्पकालिक ही क्यों न हो।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 12 को सदैव धारा 11 के साथ पढ़ें — धारा 11 कहती है कि स्वस्थ मस्तिष्क आवश्यक है, धारा 12 उसे परिभाषित करती है। न्यायालय में, अस्वस्थता का आरोप लगाने वाले पक्ष पर यह सिद्ध करने का भार होता है कि अक्षमता विशेष रूप से संविदा बनने के क्षण में विद्यमान थी; व्यक्ति की सामान्य स्थिति संबंधी चिकित्सकीय साक्ष्य प्रासंगिक तो है, परंतु अकेले निर्णायक नहीं।

sections.title: "Consent" defined
sections.raw_text: 13. "Consent" defined.—Two or more persons are said to consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 13 defines bare "consent" as consensus ad idem — a true meeting of minds where both parties understand the agreement identically. This is distinct from Section 14's "free consent"; Section 13 asks whether the parties agreed on the same thing in the same sense at all, before Section 14 asks whether that agreement was obtained fairly.
essential_elements: There must be agreement between two or more persons.
That agreement must be upon the same thing.
Both parties must understand it in the same sense (no cross-purposes).
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 13 underlies "mistake" cases (Sections 20-22): if the parties were never actually ex idem — each meant something materially different by the agreement — there may be no consent at all, and hence no agreement to found a contract on, quite apart from any question of free consent under Section 14.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 13 'सहमति' (consent) की मूल परिभाषा देती है — अर्थात् सहमति तभी मानी जाएगी जब दोनों पक्षों के मन वास्तव में एक-दूसरे से पूर्णतः मिलें (consensus ad idem)। यह धारा 14 की 'स्वतंत्र सहमति' से अलग है — धारा 13 यह पूछती है कि क्या पक्ष सिरे से एक ही बात पर एक ही अर्थ में सहमत हुए थे, जबकि धारा 14 यह पूछती है कि क्या वह सहमति निष्पक्ष ढंग से प्राप्त की गई थी।
essential_elements_hi: दो या अधिक व्यक्तियों के बीच सहमति होनी चाहिए।
वह सहमति एक ही विषय-वस्तु पर होनी चाहिए।
दोनों पक्षों को उस विषय-वस्तु को एक ही अर्थ में समझना चाहिए (विपरीत उद्देश्यों पर नहीं)।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा 13 'भूल' (mistake) से जुड़े मामलों (धारा 20-22) की नींव है — यदि पक्ष वास्तव में कभी एक ही बात पर सहमत ही नहीं हुए थे, तो हो सकता है कि कोई सहमति हो ही न, और इसलिए धारा 14 की स्वतंत्र सहमति के प्रश्न से पहले ही संविदा का आधार समाप्त हो जाए।

sections.title: "Free consent" defined
sections.raw_text:
14. "Free consent" defined.—Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by—

(1) coercion, as defined in section 15, or

(2) undue influence, as defined in section 16, or

(3) fraud, as defined in section 17, or

(4) misrepresentation, as defined in section 18, or

(5) mistake, subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21 and 22.

Consent is said to be so caused when it would not have given but for the existence of such coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.
