breakdown.plain_summary: Section 194 introduces the concept later called a 'substituted agent': when the agent's authority itself includes the power to name someone else to handle part of the business, the person so named is not a sub-agent under the agent's control — he becomes a direct agent of the principal for that part of the work, as in the auctioneer or solicitor examples.
essential_elements: The agent holds express or implied authority to name another person to act for the principal.
The agent names such a person accordingly.
That named person becomes the principal's own agent for that entrusted part of the business, not a sub-agent.
breakdown.how_to_read: The key distinction from a sub-agent (Section 191) is who that third person ultimately answers to: a sub-agent answers to the original agent, while a person appointed under this section answers directly to the principal, as his own agent.

sections.title: Agent's duty in naming such person
sections.raw_text:
In selecting such agent for his principal, an agent is bound to exercise the same amount of discretion as a man of ordinary prudence would exercise in his own case; and, if he does this, he is not responsible to the principal for the acts or negligence of the agent so selected.

Illustrations
(a) A instructs B, a merchant, to buy a ship for him. B employs a ship-surveyor of good reputation to choose a ship for A. The surveyor makes the choice negligently and the ship turns out to be unseaworthy and is lost. B is not, but the surveyor is, responsible to A.
(b) A consigns goods to B, a merchant, for sale. B, in due course, employs an auctioneer in good credit to sell the goods of A, and allows the auctioneer to receive the proceeds of the sale. The auctioneer afterwards becomes insolvent without having accounted for the proceeds. B is not responsible to A for the proceeds.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 195 sets the standard the agent must meet when exercising his Section 194 power to name a substituted agent: ordinary prudence in the selection. If he selects carefully — a reputable surveyor, a trustworthy auctioneer — he is not personally liable for that substituted agent's own later negligence or default, since that person is the principal's own agent, not the original agent's responsibility.
essential_elements: The agent selects a person to act as the principal's agent under Section 194.
The agent must exercise the discretion of a person of ordinary prudence in making that selection.
If he does so, he is not responsible to the principal for the acts or negligence of the person selected.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This protection only covers careful selection — if the agent was careless in choosing (e.g. ignoring known red flags), he could still be liable for that failure of care itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Section 194: that section decides who the substituted agent legally works for (the principal); this section decides what the original agent must do to escape liability for that person's later mistakes (exercise ordinary care in the selection itself).

sections.title: Right of person as to acts done for him without his authority; effect of ratification
sections.raw_text: Where acts are done by one person on behalf of another, but without his knowledge or authority, he may elect to ratify or to disown such acts. If he ratify them, the same effects will follow as if they had been performed by his authority.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 196 opens the ratification sub-chapter: if someone acts on your behalf without your knowledge or authorization, you get to choose afterward — accept (ratify) the act, or reject (disown) it. If you ratify, the law treats it exactly as if you had authorized it from the start.
essential_elements: An act is done by one person on behalf of another, without that other's knowledge or authority.
The person on whose behalf it was done may elect to ratify or disown the act.
If ratified, the act has the same legal effect as if originally authorized.
breakdown.how_to_read: Ratification is retroactive — think of it as authority granted backward in time, which is why the sections that follow (197-200) carefully police when and how that retroactive effect is allowed to operate.

sections.title: Ratification may be expressed or implied
sections.raw_text:
Ratification may be expressed or may be implied in the conduct of the person on whose behalf the acts are done.

Illustrations
(a) A, without authority, buys goods for B. Afterwards B sells them to C on his own account; B's conduct implies a ratification of the purchase made for him by A.
(b) A, without B's authority, lends B's money to C. Afterwards B accepts interest on the money from C. B's conduct implies a ratification of the loan.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 197 confirms ratification can happen through conduct, not just an explicit statement — if the principal, knowing the facts, acts in a way consistent only with treating the unauthorized act as his own (like selling goods bought for him, or accepting interest on a loan made in his name), that conduct itself amounts to ratification.
essential_elements: Ratification may be express (a direct statement of approval).
Or it may be implied from the conduct of the person on whose behalf the act was done.
breakdown.how_to_read: The illustrations both show the same pattern: the principal, after the fact, deals with the results of the unauthorized act as though it were his own — that's the behavioural signature of implied ratification.

sections.title: Knowledge requisite for valid ratification
sections.raw_text: No valid ratification can be made by a person whose knowledge of the facts of the case is materially defective.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 198 protects the integrity of ratification: you can't validly ratify something you didn't fully understand. If the person's knowledge of the material facts surrounding the unauthorized act is seriously deficient, any purported ratification is not valid.
essential_elements: The person ratifying must have full and accurate knowledge of the material facts of the case.
If that knowledge is materially defective, the ratification is not valid.
breakdown.how_to_read: This mirrors the free-consent logic running throughout the Act — just as genuine consent to a contract requires full knowledge, genuine ratification of someone else's unauthorized act requires the same.

sections.title: Effect of ratifying unauthorized act forming part of a transaction
sections.raw_text: A person ratifying any unauthorized act done on his behalf ratifies the whole of the transaction of which such act formed a part.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 199 prevents selective, cherry-picking ratification: you can't approve just the convenient parts of an unauthorized transaction while disowning the inconvenient parts — ratifying any part of a transaction ratifies the whole of it.
essential_elements: The unauthorized act ratified formed part of a larger transaction.
Ratifying that act ratifies the entire transaction of which it was a part.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is an 'all or nothing' rule protecting fairness to the other side of the transaction — a person can't accept the benefits while disclaiming the burdens of the very same deal.

sections.title: Ratification of unauthorized act cannot injure third person
sections.raw_text:
An act done by one person on behalf of another, without such other person's authority, which, if done with authority, would have the effect of subjecting a third person to damages, or of terminating any right or interest of a third person, cannot, by ratification, be made to have such effect.

Illustrations
(a) A, not being authorized thereto by B, demands, on behalf of B, the delivery of a chattel, the property of B, from C, who is in possession of it. This demand cannot be ratified by B, so as to make C liable for damages for his refusal to deliver.
(b) A holds a lease from B, terminable on three months' notice. C, an unauthorized person, gives notice of termination to A. The notice cannot be ratified by B, so as to be binding on A.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 200 draws a firm outer boundary on ratification's retroactive power: it cannot be used to harm an innocent third person — for example, exposing them to damages or cutting off their existing rights — in a way that wouldn't have been fair even if the act had been authorized from the start.
essential_elements: An unauthorized act, if it had been authorized, would subject a third person to damages or terminate a right/interest of theirs.
Such an act cannot be given that damaging effect merely through later ratification.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section closes the ratification sub-chapter on a protective note: the whole point of ratification is to validate the principal's own position retroactively, not to manufacture new liabilities or forfeitures for strangers to the arrangement.

sections.title: Termination of agency
sections.raw_text: An agency is terminated by the principal revoking his authority; or by the agent renouncing the business of the agency; or by the business of the agency being completed; or by either the principal or agent dying or becoming of unsound mind; or by the principal being adjudicated an insolvent under the provisions of any Act for the time being in force for the relief of insolvent debtors.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 201 opens the revocation sub-chapter with a checklist of every way an agency can end: the principal revokes it, the agent renounces it, the agency's business is completed, either party dies or becomes of unsound mind, or the principal is declared insolvent.
essential_elements: Revocation of authority by the principal.
Renunciation of the agency business by the agent.
Completion of the business of the agency.
Death or unsoundness of mind of either the principal or the agent.
Adjudication of the principal as insolvent under the law relating to insolvent debtors.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 202 (agency coupled with interest) overrides several of these grounds where the agent has his own interest in the subject-matter.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the master list; the sections immediately following (202-208) qualify, elaborate, or set procedural conditions around several of these termination grounds.

sections.title: Termination of agency, where agent has an interest in subject-matter
sections.raw_text:
Where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest.

Illustrations
(a) A gives authority to B to sell A's land, and to pay himself, out of the proceeds, the debts due to him from A. A cannot revoke this authority, nor can it be terminated by his insanity or death.
(b) A consigns 1,000 bales of cotton to B, who has made advances to him on such cotton, and desires B to sell the cotton, and to repay himself out of the price, the amount of his own advances. A cannot revoke this authority, nor is it terminated by his insanity or death.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 202 creates the important 'agency coupled with interest' exception: where the agent's own financial interest is tied up in the subject-matter (like a creditor-agent authorized to sell property and repay himself from the proceeds), the principal cannot revoke that authority to the agent's prejudice — and remarkably, it doesn't even terminate on the principal's death or insanity, unlike ordinary agency under Section 201.
essential_elements: The agent has his own interest in the property forming the subject-matter of the agency.
No express contract says otherwise.
Then the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest — surviving even events that would otherwise end an ordinary agency, such as the principal's death or insanity.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This protection can be displaced by an express contract between the parties providing otherwise.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a frequently tested exception: 'agency coupled with interest' is the standard phrase for this situation, and its hallmark is that it survives death/insanity of the principal, unlike a normal agency under Section 201.

sections.title: When principal may revoke agent's authority
sections.raw_text: The principal may, save as is otherwise provided by the last preceding section, revoke the authority given to his agent at any time before the authority has been exercised so as to bind the principal.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 203 confirms the principal's default right to revoke an agent's authority at will, at any point before that authority has actually been exercised in a way that binds the principal — subject always to the Section 202 exception for agency coupled with interest.
essential_elements: The agency is not one coupled with interest under Section 202.
The authority has not yet been exercised so as to bind the principal.
The principal may revoke the authority at any time before that point.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 202's agency-coupled-with-interest exception limits this general power to revoke.
breakdown.how_to_read: The critical timing cutoff here is 'before the authority has been exercised so as to bind the principal' — once that line is crossed, revocation is restricted, as detailed in Section 204.

sections.title: Revocation where authority has been partly exercised
sections.raw_text:
The principal cannot revoke the authority given to his agent after the authority has been partly exercised, so far as regards such acts and obligations as arise from acts already done in the agency.

Illustrations
(a) A authorizes B to buy 1,000 bales of cotton on account of A, and to pay for it out of A's moneys remaining in B's hands. B buys 1,000 bales of cotton in his own name, so as to make himself personally liable for the price. A cannot revoke B's authority so far as regards payment for the cotton.
(b) A authorizes B to buy 1,000 bales of cotton on account of A, and to pay for it out of A's moneys remaining in B's hands. B buys 1,000 bales of cotton in A's name, and so as not to render himself personally liable for the price. A can revoke B's authority to pay for the cotton.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 204 protects acts already completed under an agency: once the agent has partly exercised his authority, the principal cannot revoke as to the obligations already arising from what's already been done — though he can still revoke as to what remains undone. The illustrations show this turns on whether the agent personally bound himself (illustration (a), can't revoke as to payment) versus acted purely in the principal's name (illustration (b), can revoke).
essential_elements: The agent's authority has been partly exercised.
The principal cannot revoke as to acts and obligations already arising from what's been done so far.
Revocation remains possible for the unexecuted remainder of the authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a completed-acts protection, not a blanket bar on revocation — it only freezes what's already happened; the principal retains the power to stop anything not yet done.

sections.title: Compensation for revocation by principal, or renunciation by agent
sections.raw_text: Where there is an express or implied contract that the agency should be continued for any period of time, the principal must make compensation to the agent, or the agent to the principal, as the case may be, for any previous revocation or renunciation of the agency without sufficient cause.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 205 recognizes that while a principal can generally revoke, and an agent can generally renounce, at will, doing so without sufficient cause — when there was an express or implied agreement that the agency would last for a defined period — triggers a duty to compensate the other side for that premature ending.
essential_elements: An express or implied contract exists that the agency should continue for a defined period of time.
One party revokes (principal) or renounces (agent) the agency before that period, without sufficient cause.
That party must compensate the other for the resulting loss.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Compensation is only due where the revocation/renunciation is without sufficient cause — a justified early exit does not trigger this liability.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the agency-law analogue of damages for breach of contract: the power to revoke/renounce exists regardless (agency is never specifically enforceable), but exercising that power without cause, in breach of an agreed duration, has a price.

sections.title: Notice of revocation or renunciation
sections.raw_text: Reasonable notice must be given of such revocation or renunciation, otherwise the damage thereby resulting to the principal or the agent, as the case may be, must be made good to the one by the other.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 206 imposes a fair-warning obligation: whichever party ends the agency — principal or agent — must give reasonable notice, or else compensate the other side for any resulting damage caused by the abruptness.
essential_elements: The agency is revoked (by the principal) or renounced (by the agent).
Reasonable notice of that revocation/renunciation must be given.
Failing that, any resulting damage must be made good to the affected party.
breakdown.how_to_read: This complements Section 205: that section addresses ending the agency without sufficient cause; this one addresses ending it without adequate notice — the two can overlap, but a party could comply with one and still fall foul of the other.

sections.title: Revocation and renunciation may be expressed or implied
sections.raw_text:
Revocation and renunciation may be expressed or may be implied in the conduct of the principal or agent respectively.

Illustration
A empowers B to let A's house. Afterwards A lets it himself. This is an implied revocation of B's authority.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 207 mirrors Section 197's approach to ratification: ending an agency, too, doesn't require formal words — conduct inconsistent with the agency's continuation, like the principal personally doing the very thing he'd authorized the agent to do, implies revocation just as effectively as an explicit statement would.
essential_elements: Revocation (by the principal) or renunciation (by the agent) may be express.
Or it may be implied from the conduct of the principal or agent respectively.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section and Section 197 form a matched pair across the Act's agency chapter — both ratification and revocation/renunciation can be read from conduct, not just words, keeping the law responsive to how people actually behave.

sections.title: When termination of agent's authority takes effect as to agent, and as to third persons
sections.raw_text:
The termination of the authority of an agent does not, so far as regards the agent, take effect before it becomes known to him, or, so far as regards third persons, before it becomes known to them.

Illustrations
(a) A directs B to sell goods for him, and agrees to give B five per cent. commission on the price fetched by the goods. A afterwards, by letter, revokes B's authority. B, after the letter is sent, but before he receives it, sells the goods for 100 rupees. The sale is binding on A, and B is entitled to five rupees as his commission.
(b) A, at Madras, by letter, directs B to sell for him some cotton lying in a warehouse in Bombay, and afterwards, by letter, revokes his authority to sell, and directs B to send the cotton to Madras. B, after receiving the second letter, enters into a contract with C, who knows of the first letter, but not of the second, for the sale to him of the cotton. C pays B the money, with which B absconds. C's payment is good as against A.
(c) A directs B, his agent, to pay certain money to C. A dies, and D takes out probate to his will. B, after A's death, but before hearing of it, pays the money to C. The payment is good as against D, the executor.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 208 closes the agency-revocation chapter with a crucial timing rule: termination of an agent's authority isn't effective against the agent until he actually knows of it, and isn't effective against third persons until they know of it either. All three illustrations show acts done in ignorance of a revocation (by the agent, or by an innocent third party) still being treated as valid and binding.
essential_elements: The agent's authority has been terminated (by revocation, renunciation, death, etc.).
As against the agent, termination takes effect only once it becomes known to him.
As against third persons, termination takes effect only once it becomes known to them.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is a real-world fairness safeguard — legal termination of authority can happen instantly on paper (e.g. the moment a revocation letter is written), but its practical, binding effect is delayed until the relevant person actually learns of it, protecting those who acted in good-faith ignorance.

sections.title: Agent's duty on termination of agency by principal's death or insanity
sections.raw_text: When an agency is terminated by the principal dying or becoming of unsound mind, the agent is bound to take, on behalf of the representatives of his late principal, all reasonable steps for the protection and preservation of the interests entrusted to him.

breakdown.plain_summary: Even though the principal's death or insanity automatically ends the agency (Section 201), the agent does not get to simply walk away. The law imposes one last duty: take reasonable care of whatever was entrusted to the agent until the principal's representatives (heirs, executors, or a guardian) can take over.
essential_elements: Agency terminated by principal's death or unsoundness of mind
Agent bound to act on behalf of the late/incapacitated principal's representatives
Duty is limited to reasonable steps for protection and preservation of entrusted interests
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a residual, winding-up duty — it does not revive the agency or authorize the agent to transact new business on the principal's behalf
breakdown.how_to_read: A bridging obligation: the agency ends, but the agent's care of the principal's property does not end abruptly — read it as a duty of safekeeping until a representative steps in.

sections.title: Termination of sub-agent's authority
sections.raw_text: The termination of the authority of an agent causes the termination (subject to the rules herein contained regarding the termination of an agent's authority) of the authority of all sub-agents appointed by him.

breakdown.plain_summary: A sub-agent's authority is derivative — it flows from the agent who appointed them. So when the agent's own authority ends, every sub-agent appointed by that agent also loses authority, subject to the same termination rules (e.g., reasonable notice) that apply to agents generally.
essential_elements: Termination of an agent's authority automatically terminates sub-agents appointed by him
Subject to the same termination rules that govern agents (Sections 201-208)
breakdown.how_to_read: A chain-reaction rule: pull the agent's authority out from under a sub-agent, and the sub-agent's authority collapses with it.

sections.title: Agent's duty in conducting principal's business
sections.raw_text:
An agent is bound to conduct the business of his principal according to the directions given by the principal, or, in the absence of any such directions, according to the custom which prevails in doing business of the same kind at the place where the agent conducts such business. When the agent acts otherwise, if any loss be sustained, he must make it good to his principal, and if any profit accrues, he must account for it.

Illustrations
(a) A, an agent engaged in carrying on for B a business, in which it is the custom to invest from time to time, at interest, the moneys which may be in hand, omits to make such investment. A must make good to B the interest usually obtained by such investments.
(b) B, a broker, in whose business it is not the custom to sell on credit, sells goods of A on credit to C, whose credit at the time was very high. C, before payment, becomes insolvent. B must make good the loss to A.

breakdown.plain_summary: The agent must follow the principal's instructions to the letter. If the principal has not given instructions on a point, the agent must follow the customary practice of that kind of business at that place. Deviating from either — instructions or custom — makes the agent liable for any loss, and any profit made by the deviation must be handed over to the principal, not kept.
essential_elements: Agent bound by principal's directions, or by trade custom absent directions
Deviation causing loss makes the agent liable to make it good
Deviation yielding profit requires the agent to account for (hand over) that profit
breakdown.how_to_read: Two-tier standard: directions first, custom second. Then a symmetric consequence — loss is compensated, profit is surrendered — regardless of which way the deviation cut.

sections.title: Skill and diligence required from agent
sections.raw_text:
An agent is bound to conduct the business of the agency with as much skill as is generally possessed by persons engaged in similar business, unless the principal has notice of his want of skill. The agent is always bound to act with reasonable diligence, and to use such skill as he possesses; and to make compensation to his principal in respect of the direct consequences of his own neglect, want of skill, or misconduct, but not in respect of loss or damage which are indirectly or remotely caused by such neglect, want of skill, or misconduct.

Illustrations
(a) A, a merchant in Calcutta, has an agent, B, in London, to whom a sum of money is paid on A's account, with orders to remit. B retains the money for a considerable time. A, in consequence of not receiving the money, becomes insolvent. B is liable for the money and interest from the day on which it ought to have been paid, according to the usual rate, and for any further direct loss-as, e.g., by variation of rate of exchange-but not further.
(b) A, an agent for the sale of goods, having authority to sell on credit, sells to B on credit, without making the proper and usual enquiries as to the solvency of B. B, at the time of such sale, is insolvent. A must make compensation to his principal in respect of any loss thereby sustained.
(c) A, an insurance-broker employed by B to effect an insurance on a ship, omits to see that the usual clauses are inserted in the policy. The ship is afterwards lost. In consequence of the omission of the clauses nothing can be recovered from the underwriters. A is bound to make good the loss to B.
(d) A, a merchant in England, directs B, his agent at Bombay, who accepts the agency, to send him 100 bales of cotton by a certain ship. B, having it in his power to send the cotton, omits to do so. The ship arrives safely in England. Soon after her arrival the price of cotton rises. B is bound to make good to A the profit which he might have made by the 100 bales of cotton at the time the ship arrived, but not any profit he might have made by the subsequent rise.

breakdown.plain_summary: The agent's skill standard is objective — the general standard of persons in that line of business — unless the principal already knew the agent lacked that skill. Diligence, however, is always required, and the agent must always use whatever skill he does possess. Liability for failing this standard is capped at direct, proximate losses — not speculative or remote consequences.
essential_elements: Skill measured by the general standard in similar business, unless principal had notice of a shortfall
Reasonable diligence and use of the agent's own actual skill always required
Compensation owed only for direct consequences of neglect, want of skill, or misconduct
No liability for indirect or remote loss/damage
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the principal already knew of the agent's limited skill (notice), the general-standard benchmark does not apply to that extent
breakdown.how_to_read: A negligence-style standard with a built-in remoteness limit — first ask what standard of skill applied, then ask whether the loss claimed was a direct or merely remote consequence of falling short of it.

sections.title: Agent's accounts
sections.raw_text: An agent is bound to render proper accounts to his principal on demand.

breakdown.plain_summary: The agent must keep and produce proper accounts of the agency business whenever the principal asks for them.
essential_elements: Duty to render proper accounts
Triggered on the principal's demand
breakdown.how_to_read: Short and absolute — no qualifying conditions, just a standing duty of transparency.

sections.title: Agent's duty to communicate with principal
sections.raw_text: It is the duty of an agent, in cases of difficulty, to use all reasonable diligence in communicating with his principal, and in seeking to obtain his instructions.

breakdown.plain_summary: When the agent hits an unexpected problem or difficult situation while carrying out the agency, he must not just guess or act unilaterally — he should make a reasonably diligent effort to reach the principal and get fresh instructions before proceeding.
essential_elements: Applies in cases of difficulty arising during the agency
Agent must use reasonable diligence to communicate with the principal
Purpose is to obtain the principal's instructions
breakdown.how_to_read: A consultation duty — before improvising through a difficulty, the agent should try to check back with the principal.

sections.title: Right of principal when agent deals, on his own account, in business of agency without principal's consent
sections.raw_text:
If an agent deals on his own account in the business of the agency, without first obtaining the consent of his principal and acquainting him with all material circumstances which have come to his own knowledge on the subject, the principal may repudiate the transaction, if the case shows, either that any material fact has been dishonestly concealed from him by the agent, or that the dealings of the agent have been disadvantageous to him.

Illustrations
(a) A directs B to sell A's estate. B buys the estate for himself in the name of C. A, on discovering that B has bought the estate for himself, may repudiate the sale, if he can show that B has dishonestly concealed any material fact, or that the sale has been disadvantageous to him.
(b) A directs B to sell A's estate. B, on looking over the estate before selling it, finds a mine on the estate which is unknown to A. B informs A that he wishes to buy the estate for himself, but conceals the discovery of the mine. A allows B to buy, in ignorance of the existence of the mine. A, on discovering that B knew of the mine at the time he bought the estate, may either repudiate or adopt the sale at his option.

breakdown.plain_summary: This targets self-dealing: an agent secretly buying/selling for himself instead of genuinely acting for the principal. Unless the agent gets the principal's consent up front and discloses every material fact known to him, the principal can undo (repudiate) the deal — provided the principal can show either dishonest concealment of a material fact, or that the deal was disadvantageous.
essential_elements: Agent deals on his own account in the business of the agency
Without first obtaining the principal's consent and disclosing all material circumstances
Principal may repudiate on proof of dishonest concealment of a material fact, OR
Principal may repudiate on proof that the dealing was disadvantageous to him
exceptions_and_qualifications: Consent plus full disclosure of material circumstances up front cures the problem — the principal cannot then repudiate merely because the agent also benefited
breakdown.how_to_read: A self-dealing check: consent and disclosure are the escape hatch; without them, either dishonesty or disadvantage (either one, not both) is enough for the principal to unwind the transaction.

sections.title: Principal's right to benefit gained by agent dealing on his own account in business of agency
sections.raw_text:
If an agent, without the knowledge of his principal, deals in the business of the agency on his own account instead of on account of his principal, the principal is entitled to claim from the agent any benefit which may have resulted to him from the transaction.

Illustration A directs B, his agent, to buy a certain house for him. B tells A it cannot be bought, and buys the house for himself. A may, on discovering that B has bought the house, compel him to sell it to A at the price he gave for it.

breakdown.plain_summary: This goes further than Section 215's repudiation remedy: if the agent secretly self-deals, the principal doesn't just get to cancel the deal — the principal can actually claim the benefit that resulted, for example forcing the agent to hand over property the agent secretly bought for himself, at the price the agent paid.
essential_elements: Agent deals in the business of the agency on his own account
Without the principal's knowledge
Principal entitled to claim any resulting benefit from the transaction
breakdown.how_to_read: A disgorgement remedy — instead of merely voiding the secret deal, the law lets the principal step into the agent's shoes and take the benefit for himself.

sections.title: Agent's right of retainer out of sums received on principal's account
sections.raw_text: An agent may retain, out of any sums received on account of the principal in the business of the agency, all moneys due to himself in respect of advances made or expenses properly incurred by him in conducting such business, and also such remuneration as may be payable to him for acting as agent.

breakdown.plain_summary: Before handing over money collected on the principal's behalf, the agent can first deduct (retain) whatever the principal owes him — advances he made, proper expenses he incurred, and his agreed remuneration — and pass on only the balance.
essential_elements: Right to retain out of sums received on the principal's account
Covers: advances made, expenses properly incurred, and remuneration payable
breakdown.how_to_read: A self-help set-off — the agent doesn't need to sue separately for reimbursement; he can simply deduct it from money passing through his hands.

sections.title: Agent's duty to pay sums received for principal
sections.raw_text: Subject to such deductions, the agent is bound to pay to his principal all sums received on his account.

breakdown.plain_summary: After making the permitted deductions under Section 217, the agent must hand over the rest of the money received on the principal's behalf.
essential_elements: Subject to the Section 217 deductions
Agent must pay over all sums received on the principal's account
breakdown.how_to_read: The other half of the retainer coin — deduct what's owed to you, then remit the rest; don't hold back more than the permitted deductions.

sections.title: When agent's remuneration becomes due
sections.raw_text: In the absence of any special contract, payment for the performance of any act is not due to the agent until the completion of such act; but an agent may detain moneys received by him on account of goods sold, although the whole of the goods consigned to him for sale may not have been sold, or although the sale may not be actually complete.

breakdown.plain_summary: Absent a special agreement fixing when payment is due, the default rule is that the agent's remuneration is only payable once he has completed the act he was engaged to do. However, as a practical carve-out for sale agents, he may still hold back proportionate money already received from partial sales, even before the whole consignment is sold.
essential_elements: Default rule: remuneration due only on completion of the act, absent a special contract
Carve-out: agent may detain moneys received for goods already sold even if the full consignment is not yet sold or the sale is not fully complete
exceptions_and_qualifications: A special contract between principal and agent can displace the default completion-based timing
breakdown.how_to_read: Default timing rule, softened by a practical exception for partial sales of consigned goods.

sections.title: Agent not entitled to remuneration for business misconducted
sections.raw_text:
An agent who is guilty of misconduct in the business of the agency, is not entitled to any remuneration in respect of that part of the business which he has misconducted.

Illustrations
(a) A employs B to recover, 1,00,000 rupees from C, and to lay it out on good security. B recovers the 1,00,000 rupees; and lays out 90,000 rupees on good security, but lays out 10,000 rupees on security which he ought to have known to be bad, whereby A loses 2,000 rupees. B is entitled to remuneration for recovering the 1,00,000 rupees and for investing the 90,000 rupees. He is not entitled to any remuneration for investing the 10,000 rupees, and he must make good the 2,000 rupees to B.
(b) A employs B to recover 1,000 rupees from C. Through B's misconduct the money is not recovered. B is entitled to no remuneration for his services, and must make good the loss.

breakdown.plain_summary: Misconduct in one part of the agency work forfeits remuneration for that part specifically — the agent doesn't lose remuneration for work he did properly, but he gets nothing (and may owe damages) for the part he bungled.
essential_elements: Agent guilty of misconduct in part of the agency business
Loses remuneration only for that misconducted part
Remains entitled to remuneration for properly performed parts
breakdown.how_to_read: An apportionment rule, illustrated concretely: split the business into the well-done part and the misconducted part, and dock remuneration only for the latter.

sections.title: Agent's lien on principal's property
sections.raw_text: In the absence of any contract to the contrary, an agent is entitled to retain goods, papers and other property, whether movable or immovable of the principal received by him, until the amount due to himself for commission, disbursements and services in respect of the same has been paid or accounted for to him.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the agent's counterpart to a bailee's lien (Sections 170-171): absent a contrary agreement, the agent can hold on to the principal's goods, papers, or other property that came into his hands, until he is paid what is due to him for commission, disbursements, and services connected with that property.
essential_elements: Applies to goods, papers, and other property (movable or immovable) of the principal received by the agent
Secures amounts due for commission, disbursements, and services
Default rule — displaced by a contract to the contrary
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not apply if there is a contract to the contrary
breakdown.how_to_read: A security-interest rule — the agent's lien is a leverage device, letting him hold property hostage until paid, unless the parties agreed otherwise.

sections.title: Agent to be indemnified against consequences of lawful acts
sections.raw_text:
The employer of an agent is bound to indemnify him against the consequences of all lawful acts done by such agent in exercise of the authority conferred upon him.

Illustrations
(a) B, at Singapur, under instructions from A of Calcutta, contracts with C to deliver certain goods to him. A does not send the goods to B, and C sues B for breach of contract. B informs A of the suit, and A authorizes him to defend the suit. B defends the suit, and is compelled to pay damages and costs, and incurs expenses. A is liable to B for such damages, costs and expenses.
(b) B, a broker at Calcutta, by the orders of A, a merchant there, contracts with C for the purchase of 10 casks of oil for A. Afterwards A refuses to receive the oil, and C sues B. B informs A, who repudiates the contract altogether. B defends, but unsuccessfully, and has to pay damages and costs and incurs expenses. A is liable to B for such damages, costs and expenses.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the agent, acting within his authority, does something lawful and it ends up costing him money (damages, costs, expenses), the principal must reimburse him. This protects agents from bearing the financial fallout of properly authorized conduct.
essential_elements: Applies to lawful acts done by the agent in exercise of conferred authority
Principal (employer) bound to indemnify the agent against the consequences
breakdown.how_to_read: A baseline protection for agents: act lawfully and within authority, and the principal absorbs the downstream cost.

sections.title: Agent to be indemnified against consequences of acts done in good faith
sections.raw_text:
Where one person employs another to do an act, and the agent does the act in good faith, the employer is liable to indemnify the agent against the consequences of that act, though it cause an injury to the rights of third persons.

Illustrations
(a) A, a decree-holder and entitled to execution of B's goods, requires the officer of the Court to seize certain goods, representing them to be the goods of B. The officer seizes the goods, and is sued by C, the true owner of the goods. A is liable to indemnify the officer for the sum which he is compelled to pay to C, in consequence of obeying A's directions.
(b) B, at the request of A, sells goods in the possession of A, but which A had no right to dispose of, B does not know this, and hands over the proceeds of the sale to A. Afterwards C, the true owner of the goods, sues B and recovers the value of the goods and costs. A is liable to indemnify B for what he has been compelled to pay to C, and for B's own expenses.
key_terms: injury to rights of third persons

breakdown.plain_summary: Even where the agent's good-faith act ends up injuring some third person's rights (e.g., the principal turns out not to have had the right to the goods), the principal must still indemnify the agent for the resulting liability and expenses — as long as the agent acted in good faith on the principal's instructions.
essential_elements: Agent does the act in good faith
Act causes injury to the rights of a third person
Employer/principal is liable to indemnify the agent against the consequences
breakdown.how_to_read: Good faith is the key qualifier here — it extends indemnity protection even to acts that turn out to wrong a third party, so long as the agent didn't know better.

sections.title: Non-liability of employer of agent to do a criminal act
sections.raw_text:
Where one person employs another to do an act which is criminal, the employer is not liable to the agent, either upon an express or an implied promise, to indemnify him against the consequences of that act.

Illustrations
(a) A employs B to beat C, and agrees to indemnify him against all consequences of the act. B thereupon beats C, and has to pay damages to C for so doing. A is not liable to indemnify B for those damages.
(b) B, the proprietor of a newspaper, publishes, at A's request, a libel upon C in the paper, and A agrees to indemnify B against the consequences of the publication, and all costs and damages of any action in respect thereof. B is sued by C and has to pay damages, and also incurs expenses. A is not liable to B upon the indemnity.

breakdown.plain_summary: The indemnity protections of Sections 222 and 223 have a hard limit: if the act the agent was employed to do is itself criminal, the principal cannot be forced to indemnify the agent for the consequences — even if the principal expressly promised to do so. Courts will not enforce an indemnity for crime.
essential_elements: Act employed to be done is criminal
Employer not liable to indemnify — even under an express promise to do so
Also excludes indemnity arising by implied promise
breakdown.how_to_read: A public-policy override — no indemnity for criminal acts, express agreement notwithstanding; this is the counterpoint to Sections 222-223's general indemnity rules.

sections.title: Compensation to agent for injury caused by principal's neglect
sections.raw_text:
The principal must make compensation to his agent in respect of injury caused to such agent by the principal's neglect or want of skill.

Illustration A employs B as a bricklayer in building a house, and puts up the scaffolding himself. The scaffolding is unskilfully put up, and B is in consequence hurt. A must make compensation to B.

breakdown.plain_summary: The duty of care runs both ways: just as the agent owes the principal skill and diligence, the principal owes the agent compensation if the principal's own neglect or lack of skill causes the agent physical or other injury while carrying out the agency.
essential_elements: Injury caused to the agent
Caused by the principal's neglect or want of skill
Principal must compensate the agent
breakdown.how_to_read: A mirror-image duty to Section 212 — this time it is the principal's carelessness that triggers compensation, owed to the agent.

sections.title: Enforcement and consequences of agent's contracts
sections.raw_text:
Contracts entered into through an agent, and obligations arising from acts done by an agent, may be enforced in the same manner, and will have the same legal consequences, as if the contracts had been entered into and the acts done by the principal in person.

Illustrations
(a) A buys goods from B, knowing that he is an agent for their sale, but not knowing who is the principal. B's principal is the person entitled to claim from A the price of the goods, and A cannot, in a suit by the principal, set-off against that claim a debt due to himself from B.
(b) A, being B's agent, with authority to receive money on his behalf, receives from C a sum of money due to B. C is discharged of his obligation to pay the sum in question to B.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the foundational rule of agency law: a contract made through a duly authorized agent binds and benefits the principal exactly as if the principal had personally entered into it. It can be enforced by or against the principal, and third parties are bound in dealing with the agent as they would be in dealing directly with the principal.
essential_elements: Contracts entered into through an agent
Obligations arising from the agent's acts
Enforced in the same manner, with the same legal consequences, as if the principal acted in person
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the master rule underlying the entire chapter — agency 'transmits' legal effect from agent to principal as though there were no intermediary at all.

sections.title: Principal how far bound, when agent exceeds authority
sections.raw_text:
When an agent does more than he is authorized to do, and when the part of what he does, which is within his authority, can be separated from the part which is beyond his authority, so much only of what he does as is within his authority is binding as between him and his principal.

Illustration A, being owner of a ship and cargo, authorizes B to procure an insurance for 4,000 rupees on the ship. B procures a policy for 4,000 rupees on the ship, and another for the like sum on the cargo. A is bound to pay the premium for the policy on the ship, but not the premium for the policy on the cargo.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the agent's excess act can be cleanly separated from the authorized act, the principal is bound only by the authorized part; the unauthorized excess simply doesn't bind the principal, but the valid part stands on its own.
essential_elements: Agent does more than authorized
Authorized and unauthorized parts are separable
Only the authorized part binds the principal
breakdown.how_to_read: The first half of a two-part rule (paired with Section 228) turning on separability — sever what you can, and hold the principal only to the authorized slice.

sections.title: Principal not bound when excess of agent's authority is not separable
sections.raw_text:
Where an agent does more than he is authorized to do, and what he does beyond the scope of his authority cannot be separated from what is within it, the principal is not bound to recognize the transaction.

Illustration A authorizes B to buy 500 sheep for him. B buys 500 sheep and 200 lambs for one sum of 6,000 rupees. A may repudiate the whole transaction.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the excess cannot be cleanly severed from the authorized part (e.g., a single lump-sum deal covering both), the principal is entitled to reject the entire transaction — not just the excess portion.
essential_elements: Agent exceeds authority
Excess is not separable from the authorized part
Principal not bound to recognize the transaction at all
breakdown.how_to_read: The flip side of Section 227 — when you cannot cleanly split authorized from unauthorized, the whole deal falls, and the principal may repudiate it entirely.

sections.title: Consequences of notice given to agent
sections.raw_text:
Any notice given to or information obtained by the agent, provided it be given or obtained in the course of the business transacted by him for the principal, shall, as between the principal and third parties, have the same legal consequences as if it had been given to or obtained by the principal.

Illustrations
(a) A is employed by B to buy from C certain goods, of which C is the apparent owner, and buys them accordingly. In the course of the treaty for the sale, A learns that the goods really belonged to D, but B is ignorant of that fact. B is not entitled to set-off a debt owing to him from C against the price of the goods.
(b) A is employed by B to buy from C goods of which C is the apparent owner. A was, before he was so employed, a servant of C, and then learnt that the goods really belonged to D, but B is ignorant of that fact. In spite of the knowledge of his agent, B may set-off against the price of the goods a debt owing to him from C.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the doctrine of imputed notice: knowledge the agent picks up while transacting the principal's business is treated, as against third parties, as if the principal himself knew it — even if the principal in fact had no idea. But knowledge the agent acquired outside that course of business (e.g., from an earlier, unrelated role, as in Illustration (b)) is not imputed.
essential_elements: Notice given to, or information obtained by, the agent
Must be in the course of the business transacted for the principal
Treated as if given to or obtained by the principal himself, as against third parties
exceptions_and_qualifications: Knowledge acquired by the agent outside the course of the relevant agency business is not imputed to the principal (Illustration (b))
breakdown.how_to_read: An imputation rule — trace whether the agent's knowledge arose inside or outside the specific agency transaction; only 'inside' knowledge binds the principal.

sections.title: Agent cannot personally enforce, nor be bound by, contracts on behalf of principal

breakdown.plain_summary: The default rule is that the agent is merely a conduit — he can neither sue on, nor be sued on, contracts he made for the principal. But the section flags three situations where the opposite is presumed: the principal is a foreign merchant, the agent doesn't name the principal, or the disclosed principal cannot be sued (e.g., diplomatic immunity). In these cases, the agent is presumed personally liable/entitled unless shown otherwise.
essential_elements: Default: agent cannot personally sue or be sued on the principal's contracts
Displaced by an actual contract to the contrary
Also presumed displaced in three situations: foreign-resident merchant principal, undisclosed principal, or a disclosed principal who cannot be sued
exceptions_and_qualifications: The three listed situations are themselves presumptions, rebuttable by evidence of a contrary intention
breakdown.how_to_read: Default non-liability of the agent, with three statutory presumptions flipping that default — treat the list as situations practitioners must specifically check for when deciding whom to sue.

sections.title: Rights of parties to a contract made by agent not disclosed
sections.raw_text: If an agent makes a contract with a person who neither knows, nor has reason to suspect, that he is an agent, his principal may require the performance of the contract; but the other contracting party has, as against the principal, the same rights as he would have had as against the agent if the agent had been principal. If the principal discloses himself before the contract is completed, the other contracting party may refuse to fulfil the contract, if he can show that, if he had known who was the principal in the contract, or if he had known that the agent was not a principal, he would not have entered into the contract.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the other party has no idea (and no reason to suspect) they're dealing with an agent, the real principal can still step in and demand performance — but the other party keeps all the defences/rights they would have had against the agent personally. And if the principal reveals himself before the deal is done, the other party can back out if they can show they would never have contracted had they known the true principal, or known it wasn't a principal-to-principal deal.
essential_elements: Agent contracts with a party unaware (and with no reason to suspect) that he is an agent
Principal may require performance of the contract
Other party retains, against the principal, the same rights as against the agent
If principal discloses before completion, other party may refuse performance on proof that knowledge of the true principal (or of the agency) would have changed their decision to contract
breakdown.how_to_read: Balances the undisclosed principal's right to step in against the other party's reliance interest — the other party is not worse off than if they'd known they were dealing with an agent from the start.

sections.title: Performance of contract with agent supposed to be principal
sections.raw_text:
Where one man makes a contract with another, neither knowing nor having reasonable ground to suspect that the other is an agent, the principal, if he requires the performance of the contract, can only obtain such performance subject to the rights and obligations subsisting between the agent and the other party to the contract.

Illustration A, who owes 500 rupees to B, sells 1,000 rupees worth of rice to B. A is acting as agent for C in the transaction, but B has no knowledge nor reasonable ground of suspicion that such is the case. C cannot compel B to take the rice without allowing him to set-off A's debt.

breakdown.plain_summary: When the undisclosed principal wants to step in and enforce the contract, he takes it subject to any rights (like a set-off) that had already accrued between the agent and the other party — the principal cannot claim a cleaner position than the agent himself had.
essential_elements: Contract made without knowledge or reasonable suspicion of agency
Principal enforcing the contract takes it subject to rights/obligations already existing between the agent and the other party
breakdown.how_to_read: A step-into-the-agent's-shoes rule — the principal's enforcement right is capped by whatever equities (like set-offs) already existed between the agent and the third party.

sections.title: Right of person dealing with agent personally liable
sections.raw_text:
In cases where the agent is personally liable, a person dealing with him may hold either him or his principal, or both of them, liable.

Illustration A enters into a contract with B to sell him 100 bales of cotton, and afterwards discovers that B was acting as agent for C. A may sue either B or C, or both, for the price of the cotton.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where circumstances make the agent personally liable (per the exceptions in Section 230), the other party isn't forced to choose only one target — they may sue the agent, the principal, or both.
essential_elements: Applies only where the agent is personally liable in the first place
Other party may hold the agent, the principal, or both liable
breakdown.how_to_read: A procedural flexibility rule for the claimant — options, not an either/or election, when the agent happens to be personally liable.

sections.title: Consequence of inducing agent or principal to act on belief that principal or agent will be held exclusively liable
sections.raw_text: When a person who has made a contract with an agent induces the agent to act upon the belief that the principal only will be held liable, or induces the principal to act upon the belief that the agent only will be held liable, he cannot afterwards hold liable the agent or principal respectively.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is an estoppel-style rule: if the third party deliberately leads the agent to believe only the principal will be pursued (or leads the principal to believe only the agent will be pursued), the third party is then held to that representation and loses the right to later go after the party they excluded.
essential_elements: Third party induces agent to believe only the principal will be held liable, OR induces principal to believe only the agent will be held liable
Third party thereafter cannot hold liable the party he induced to be excluded
breakdown.how_to_read: An estoppel check on Section 233's flexibility — the freedom to sue either or both is lost if the claimant already committed, by conduct, to pursuing only one of them.

sections.title: Liability of pretended agent
sections.raw_text: A person untruly representing himself to be the authorized agent of another, and thereby inducing a third person to deal with him as such agent, is liable, if his alleged employer does not ratify his acts, to make compensation to the other in respect of any loss or damage which he has incurred by so dealing.

breakdown.plain_summary: Someone who falsely claims to be another person's authorized agent, and thereby gets a third party to deal with them on that false basis, is personally liable to compensate that third party for any loss — unless the person they claimed to represent chooses to ratify (adopt) the unauthorized acts after the fact.
essential_elements: Untrue representation of being an authorized agent
Induces a third person to deal with the pretender as such an agent
No ratification by the alleged employer
Pretender liable to compensate the third party for loss or damage
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the alleged employer ratifies the pretended agent's acts, the pretender escapes this liability
breakdown.how_to_read: A fraud-adjacent liability rule for fake agents, with ratification (Sections 196-200) as the escape valve if the supposed principal chooses to adopt the acts anyway.

sections.title: Person falsely contracting as agent not entitled to performance
sections.raw_text: A person with whom a contract has been entered into in the character of agent, is not entitled to require the performance of it, if he was in reality acting, not as agent, but on his own account.

breakdown.plain_summary: If someone pretends to contract as an agent for another, but was actually acting for himself all along, he cannot later turn around and demand performance of that contract in his own right — his false representation of agency bars him from enforcing it as a principal.
essential_elements: Contract entered into in the character of an agent
Person was in reality acting on his own account, not as agent
Not entitled to require performance of the contract
breakdown.how_to_read: A companion to Section 235, from the other direction — this bars the false 'agent' from claiming performance for himself, rather than making him liable to a third party.

sections.title: Liability of principal inducing belief that agent's unauthorized acts were authorized
sections.raw_text:
When an agent has, without authority, done acts or incurred obligations to third persons on behalf of his principal, the principal is bound by such acts or obligations, if he has by his words or conduct induced such third persons to believe that such acts and obligations were within the scope of the agent's authority.

Illustrations
(a) A consigns goods to B for sale, and gives him instructions not to sell under a fixed price. C, being ignorant of B's instructions, enters into a contract with B to buy the goods at a price lower than the reserved price. A is bound by the contract.
(b) A entrusts B with negotiable instruments endorsed in blank. B sells them to C in violation of private orders from A. The sale is good.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the doctrine of apparent (or 'ostensible') authority: even where the agent secretly exceeded his actual private instructions, the principal is still bound if the principal's own words or conduct made it reasonably appear to third parties that the agent had that authority. The third party's ignorance of secret internal limits is protected.
essential_elements: Agent acts without actual authority, or incurs obligations, on the principal's behalf
Principal, by words or conduct, induced third persons to believe the act was within the agent's authority
Principal bound by such acts/obligations
exceptions_and_qualifications: Private, undisclosed instructions limiting the agent's authority do not bind third parties who reasonably believed the agent had full authority
breakdown.how_to_read: The apparent-authority doctrine — look at what the principal outwardly held out to the world, not just the private instructions given to the agent behind the scenes.

sections.title: Effect, on agreement, of misrepresentation or fraud, by agent
sections.raw_text:
Misrepresentation made, or frauds committed, by agents acting in the course of their business for their principals, have the same effect on agreements made by such agents as if such misrepresentations or frauds had been made or committed by the principals; but misrepresentations made, or frauds committed, by agents, in matters which do not fall within their authority, do not affect their principals.

Illustrations
(a) A, being B's agent for the sale of goods, induces C to buy them by a misrepresentation, which he was not authorized by B to make. The contract is voidable, as between B and C, at the option of C.
(b) A, the captain of B's ship, signs bills of lading without having received on board the goods mentioned therein. The bills of lading are void as between B and the pretended cosignor.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes out the Agency chapter by fixing how an agent's dishonesty or false statements affect the principal. If the agent's misrepresentation or fraud happens in the course of doing the principal's business, it is treated exactly as if the principal made it — even if the principal did not authorize that specific misstatement (Illustration (a) shows the resulting contract is voidable at the innocent third party's option). But fraud or misrepresentation in matters entirely outside the agent's authority does not bind the principal at all.
essential_elements: Misrepresentation or fraud committed by the agent in the course of business for the principal
Treated as if committed by the principal himself
Exception: misrepresentation/fraud in matters not falling within the agent's authority does not affect the principal
